entries.0f744028b5e1a3f1e49c59a0994eaaa555bbe863: <div sID="gen6347" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="19" osisID="2Sam.19" sID="2Sam.19"/> <div eID="gen6347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6348" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6349" type="x-p"/> We left David's army in triumph and yet David himself in tears: now here we have, I. His return to himself, by the persuasion of Joab, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.1-2Sam.19.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. His return to his kingdom from his present banishment. 1. The men of Israel were forward of themselves to bring him back, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.9-2Sam.19.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>. 2. The men of Judah were dealt with by David's agents to do it (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.11-2Sam.19.14">ver. 11-14</reference>) and did it, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.15">ver. 15</reference>. III. At the king's coming over Jordan, Shimei's treason is pardoned (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.16-2Sam.19.23">ver. 16-23</reference>), Mephibosheth's failure is excused (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.24-2Sam.19.30">ver. 24-30</reference>), and Barzillai's kindness is thankfully owned, and recompensed to his son, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.31-2Sam.19.39">ver. 31-39</reference>. IV. The men of Israel quarrelled with the men of Judah, for not calling them to the ceremony of the king's restoration, which occasioned a new rebellion, an account of which we have in the next chapter, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.40-2Sam.19.43">ver. 40-43</reference>.
entries.86b25504bbee62923162cfacb6ddd7232202aa80: <div eID="gen6349" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6348" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Joab's Reproof of David. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1023.)</title> <div sID="gen6350" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it was told Joab, Behold, the king weepeth and mourneth for Absalom. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the victory that day was <hi type="italic">turned</hi> into mourning unto all the people: for the people heard say that day how the king was grieved for his son. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the people gat them by stealth that day into the city, as people being ashamed steal away when they flee in battle. <hi type="super">4</hi> But the king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son! <hi type="super">5</hi> And Joab came into the house to the king, and said, Thou hast shamed this day the faces of all thy servants, which this day have saved thy life, and the lives of thy sons and of thy daughters, and the lives of thy wives, and the lives of thy concubines; <hi type="super">6</hi> In that thou lovest thine enemies, and hatest thy friends. For thou hast declared this day, that thou regardest neither princes nor servants: for this day I perceive, that if Absalom had lived, and all we had died this day, then it had pleased thee well. <hi type="super">7</hi> Now therefore arise, go forth, and speak comfortably unto thy servants: for I swear by the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , if thou go not forth, there will not tarry one with thee this night: and that will be worse unto thee than all the evil that befel thee from thy youth until now. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then the king arose, and sat in the gate. And they told unto all the people, saying, Behold, the king doth sit in the gate. And all the people came before the king: for Israel had fled every man to his tent. <div eID="gen6350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6351" type="x-p"/> Soon after the messengers had brought the news of the defeat and death of Absalom to the court of Mahanaim, Joab and his victorious army followed, to grace the king's triumphs and receive his further orders. Now here we are told, <div eID="gen6351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6352" type="x-p"/> I. What a damp and disappointment it was to them to find the king in tears for Absalom's death, which they construed as a token of displeasure against them for what they had done, whereas they expected him to have met them with joy and thanks for their good services: <hi type="italic">It was told Joab,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.1">v. 1</reference>. The report of it ran through the army (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">how the king was grieved for his son.</hi> The people will take particular notice what their princes say and do. The more eyes we have upon us, and the greater our influence is, the more need we have to speak and act wisely and to govern our passions strictly. When they came to the city they found the king in close mourning, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.4">v. 4</reference>. He covered his face, and would not so much as look up, nor take any notice of the generals when they attended him. It could not but surprise them to find, 1. How the king proclaimed his passion, of which he ought to have been ashamed, and which he would have striven to smother and conceal if he had consulted either his reputation for courage, which was lessened by his mean submission to the tyranny of so absurd a passion, or his interest in the people, which would be prejudiced by his discountenancing what was done in zeal for his honour and the public safety. Yet see how he avows his grief: <hi type="italic">He cries with a loud voice, O my son Absalom!</hi> "My servants have all come home safe, but where is my son? He is dead; and, dying in sin, I fear he is lost for ever. I cannot now say, <hi type="italic">I shall go to him,</hi> for my soul shall not be gathered with such sinners; what shall be done for thee, <hi type="italic">O Absalom! my son, my son!</hi>" 2. How he prolonged his passion, even till the army had come up to him, which must be some time after he received the first intelligence. If he had contented himself with giving vent to his passion for an hour or two when he first heard the news, it would have been excusable, but to continue it thus for so bad a son as Absalom, like Jacob for so good a son as Joseph, with a resolution to go to the grave mourning and to stain his triumphs with his tears, was very unwise and very unworthy. Now see how ill this was taken by the people. They were loth to blame the king, for <hi type="italic">whatever he did used to please them</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.36">ch. iii. 36</reference>), but they took it as a great mortification to them. <hi type="italic">Their victory was turned into mourning,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.2">v. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">They stole into the city as men ashamed,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.3">v. 3</reference>. In compliment to their sovereign, they would not rejoice in that which they perceived so afflictive to him, and yet they could not but be uneasy that they were thus obliged to conceal their joy. Superiors ought not to put such hardships as these on their inferiors. <div eID="gen6352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6353" type="x-p"/> II. How plainly and vehemently Joab reproved David for this indiscreet management of himself in this critical juncture. David never more needed the hearts of his subjects than now, nor was ever more concerned to secure his interest in their affections; and therefore whatever tended to disoblige them now was the most impolitic thing he could do, and the greatest wrong imaginable to his friends that adhered to him. Joab therefore censures him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.5-2Sam.19.7">v. 5-7</reference>. He speaks a great deal of reason, but not with the respect and deference which he owed to his prince. <hi type="italic">Is is fit to say to a king, Thou art wicked?</hi> A plain case may be fairly pleaded with those that are above us, and they may be reproved for what they do amiss, but it must not be done with rudeness and insolence. David did indeed need to be roused and alarmed; and Joab thought it no time to dally with him. If superiors do that which is foolish, they must neither think it strange nor take it ill if their inferiors tell them of it, perhaps too bluntly. 1. Joab magnifies the services of David's soldiers: "<hi type="italic">This day they have saved thy life,</hi> and therefore deserve to be taken notice of, and have reason to resent it if they be not." It is implied that Absalom, whom he honoured with his tears, sought his ruin and the ruin of his family, while those whom by his tears he puts a slight upon were such as preserved from ruin him and all that was dear to him. Great mischiefs have arisen to princes from the contempt of great merits. 2. He aggravates the discouragement David had given them: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast shamed their faces;</hi> for, while they have shown such a value for thy life, thou hast shown no value for theirs, but preferrest a spoiled wicked youth, a false traitor to his king and country, whom we are happily rid of, before all thy wise counsellors, brave commanders, and loyal subjects. What can be more absurd than to love thy enemies and hate thy friends?" 3. He advises him to present himself immediately at the head of his troops, to smile upon them, welcome them home, congratulate their success, and return them thanks for their services. Even those that may be commanded yet expect to be thanked when they do well, and ought to be. 4. He threatens him with another rebellion if he would not do this, intimating that rather than serve so ungrateful a prince he himself would head a revolt from him, and then (so confident is Joab of his own interest in the people) "<hi type="italic">there will not tarry with thee one man.</hi> If I go, they will go. Thou hast now nothing to mourn for: but, if thou persist, I will give thee something to mourn for (as Josephus expresses it) with a true and more bitter mourning." <div eID="gen6353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6354" type="x-p"/> III. How prudently and mildly David took the reproof and counsel given him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.8">v. 8</reference>. He shook off his grief, anointed his head, and washed his face, that he might not appear unto men to mourn, and then made his appearance in public in the gate, which was as the guild-hall of the city. Hither the people flocked to him to congratulate his and their safety, and all was well. Note, When we are convinced of a fault, we must amend, though we are told of it by our inferiors, and indecently, or in heat and passion.
entries.245ad73459492e02c62a3da1778c37098fe9d627: <div eID="gen6354" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Return to the Jordan. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1023.)</title> <div sID="gen6355" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And all the people were at strife throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, The king saved us out of the hand of our enemies, and he delivered us out of the hand of the Philistines; and now he is fled out of the land for Absalom. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Absalom, whom we anointed over us, is dead in battle. Now therefore why speak ye not a word of bringing the king back? <hi type="super">11</hi> And king David sent to Zadok and to Abiathar the priests, saying, Speak unto the elders of Judah, saying, Why are ye the last to bring the king back to his house? seeing the speech of all Israel is come to the king, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to his house. <hi type="super">12</hi> Ye <hi type="italic">are</hi> my brethren, ye <hi type="italic">are</hi> my bones and my flesh: wherefore then are ye the last to bring back the king? <hi type="super">13</hi> And say ye to Amasa, <hi type="italic">Art</hi> thou not of my bone, and of my flesh? God do so to me, and more also, if thou be not captain of the host before me continually in the room of Joab. <hi type="super">14</hi> And he bowed the heart of all the men of Judah, even as <hi type="italic">the heart of</hi> one man; so that they sent <hi type="italic">this word</hi> unto the king, Return thou, and all thy servants. <hi type="super">15</hi> So the king returned, and came to Jordan. And Judah came to Gilgal, to go to meet the king, to conduct the king over Jordan. <div eID="gen6355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6356" type="x-p"/> It is strange that David did not immediately upon the defeat and dispersion of Absalom's forces march with all expedition back to Jerusalem, to regain the possession of his capital city, while the rebels were in confusion and before they could rally again. What occasion was there to bring him back? Could not he himself go back with the victorious army he had with him in Gilead? He could, no doubt; but, 1. He would go back as a prince, with the consent and unanimous approbation of the people, and not as a conqueror forcing his way: he would restore their liberties, and not take occasion to seize them, or encroach upon them. 2. He would go back in peace and safety, and be sure that he should meet with no difficulty or opposition in his return, and therefore would be satisfied that the people were well-affected to have him before he would stir. 3. He would go back in honour, and like himself, and therefore would go back, not at the head of his forces, but in the arms of his subjects; for the prince that has wisdom and goodness enough to make himself his people's darling, without doubt, looks greater and makes a much better figure than the prince that has strength enough to make himself his people's terror. It is resolved therefore that David must be brought back to Jerusalem his own city, and his own house there, with some ceremony, and here we have that matter concerted. <div eID="gen6356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6357" type="x-p"/> I. The men of Israel (that is, the ten tribes) were the first that talked of it, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.9-2Sam.19.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. The people were at strife about it; it was the great subject of discourse and dispute throughout all the country. Some perhaps opposed it: "Let him either come back himself or stay where he is;" others appeared zealous for it, and reasoned as follows here, to further the design, 1. That David had formerly helped them, had fought their battles, subdued their enemies, and done them much service, and therefore it was a shame that he should continue banished from their country who had been so great a benefactor to it. Note, Good services done to the public, though they may be forgotten for a while, yet will be remembered again when men come to their right minds. 2. That Absalom had now disappointed them. "We were foolishly sick of the cedar, and chose the branch to reign over us; but we have had enough of him: he is consumed, and we narrowly escaped being consumed with him. Let us therefore return to our allegiance, and think of bringing the king back." Perhaps this was all the strife among them, not a dispute whether the king should be brought back or no (all agreed it was to be done), but whose fault is was that it was not done. As is usual in such cases, every one justified himself and blamed his neighbour. The people laid the fault on the elders, and the elders on the people, and one tribe upon another. Mutual excitements to the doing of a good work are laudable, but not mutual accusations for the not doing of it; for usually when public services are neglected all sides must share in the blame; every one might do more than he does, in the reformation of manners, the healing of divisions, and the like. <div eID="gen6357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6358" type="x-p"/> II. The men of Judah, by David's contrivance, were the first that did it. It is strange that they, being David's own tribe, were not so forward as the rest. David had intelligence of the good disposition of all the rest towards him, but nothing from Judah, though he had always been particularly careful of them. But we do not always find the most kindness from those from whom we have most reason to expect it. Yet David would not return till he knew the sense of his own tribe. <hi type="italic">Judah was his lawgiver,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.60.7">Ps. lx. 7</reference>. That his way home might be the more clear, 1. He employed Zadok and Abiathar, the two chief priests, to treat with the elders of Judah, and to excite them to give the king an invitation back to his house, even to his house, which was the glory of their tribe, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.11-2Sam.19.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. No men more proper to negociate this affair than the two priests, who were firm to David's interest, were prudent men, and had great influence with the people. Perhaps the men of Judah were remiss and careless, and did it not, because nobody put them on to do it, and then it was proper to stir them up to it. Many will follow in a good work who will not lead: it is a pity that they should continue idle for want of being spoken to. Or perhaps they were so sensible of the greatness of the provocation they had given to David, by joining with Absalom, that they were afraid to bring him back, despairing of his favour; he therefore warrants his agents to assure them of it, with this reason: "<hi type="italic">You are my brethren, my bone and my flesh,</hi> and therefore I cannot be severe with you." The Son of David has been pleased to call us <hi type="italic">brethren, his bone and his flesh,</hi> which encourages us to hope that we shall find favour with him. Or perhaps they were willing to see what the rest of the tribes would do before they stirred, with which they are here upbraided: "The speech of all Israel has come to the king to invite him back, and shall Judah be the last, that should have been the first? Where is now the celebrated bravery of that royal tribe? Where is its loyalty?" Note, We should be stirred up to that which is great and good by the examples both of our ancestors and of our neighbours, and by the consideration of our rank. Let not the first in dignity be last in duty. 2. He particularly courted into his interest Amasa, who had been Absalom's general, but was his own nephew as well as Joab, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.13">v. 13</reference>. He owns him for his kinsman, and promises him that, if he will appear for him now, he will make him captain-general of all his forces in the room of Joab, will not only pardon him (which, it may be, Amasa questioned), but prefer him. Sometimes there is nothing lost in purchasing the friendship of one that has been an enemy. Amasa's interest might do David good service at this juncture. But, if David did wisely for himself in designating Amasa for this post (Joab having now grown intolerably haughty), he did not do kindly by Amasa in letting his design be known, for it occasioned his death by Joab's hand, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.10">ch. xx. 10</reference>. 3. The point was hereby gained. He bowed the heart of the men of Judah to pass a vote, <hi type="italic">nemine contradicente—unanimously,</hi> for the recall of the king, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.14">v. 14</reference>. God's providence, by the priests' persuasions and Amasa's interest, brought them to this resolve. David stirred not till he received this invitation, and then he came as far back as Jordan, at which river they were to meet him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.15">v. 15</reference>. Our Lord Jesus will rule in those that invite him to the throne in their hearts and not till he be invited. He first bows the heart and makes it willing in the day of his power, and then <hi type="italic">rules in the midst of his enemies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.2-Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 2, 3</reference>.
entries.a775a8dfa3583be51508df9b82a6da4a24d198c2: <div eID="gen6358" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Pardons Shimei. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1023.)</title> <div sID="gen6359" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And Shimei the son of Gera, a Benjamite, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> of Bahurim, hasted and came down with the men of Judah to meet king David. <hi type="super">17</hi> And <hi type="italic">there were</hi> a thousand men of Benjamin with him, and Ziba the servant of the house of Saul, and his fifteen sons and his twenty servants with him; and they went over Jordan before the king. <hi type="super">18</hi> And there went over a ferry boat to carry over the king's household, and to do what he thought good. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king, as he was come over Jordan; <hi type="super">19</hi> And said unto the king, Let not my lord impute iniquity unto me, neither do thou remember that which thy servant did perversely the day that my lord the king went out of Jerusalem, that the king should take it to his heart. <hi type="super">20</hi> For thy servant doth know that I have sinned: therefore, behold, I am come the first this day of all the house of Joseph to go down to meet my lord the king. <hi type="super">21</hi> But Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered and said, Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's anointed? <hi type="super">22</hi> And David said, What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah, that ye should this day be adversaries unto me? shall there any man be put to death this day in Israel? for do not I know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> this day king over Israel? <hi type="super">23</hi> Therefore the king said unto Shimei, Thou shalt not die. And the king sware unto him. <div eID="gen6359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6360" type="x-p"/> Perhaps Jordan was never passed with so much solemnity, nor with so many remarkable occurrences, as it was now, since Israel passed it under Joshua. David, in his afflictive flight, remembered God particularly <hi type="italic">from the land of Jordan</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.6">Ps. xlii. 6</reference>), and now that land, more than any other, was graced with the glories of his return. David's soldiers furnished themselves with accommodations for their passage over this river, but, for his own family, <hi type="italic">a ferry-boat</hi> was sent on purpose, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.18">v. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">A fleet of boats,</hi> say some; <hi type="italic">a bridge of boats was made,</hi> say others; the best convenience they had to serve him with. Two remarkable persons met him on the banks of Jordan, both of whom had abused him wretchedly when he was in his flight. <div eID="gen6360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6361" type="x-p"/> I. Ziba, who had abused him with his fair tongue, and by accusing his master, had obtained from the king a grant of his estate, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.4">ch. xvi. 4</reference>. A greater abuse he could not have done him, than, by imposing upon his credulity, to draw him in to do a thing so unkind to the son of his friend Jonathan. He comes now, with a retinue of sons and servants, to meet the king (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.17">v. 17</reference>), that he may obtain the king's favour, and so come off the better when Mephibosheth shall shortly undeceive him, and clear himself, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.26">v. 26</reference>. <div eID="gen6361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6362" type="x-p"/> II. Shimei, who had abused him with his foul tongue, railed at him, and cursed him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.5">ch. xvi. 5</reference>. If David had been defeated, no doubt he would have continued to trample upon him, and have gloried in what he had done; but now that he sees him coming home in triumph, and returning to his throne, he thinks it his interest to make his peace with him. Those who now slight and abuse the Son of David would be glad to make their peace too when he shall come in his glory; but it will be too late. Shimei, to recommend himself to the king, 1. Came with good company, with the men of Judah, as one in their interest. 2. He brought a regiment of the men of Benjamin with him, 1000, of which perhaps he was chiliarch, or commander-in-chief, offering his own and their service to the king; or perhaps they were volunteers, whom by his interest he had got together to meet the king, which was the more obliging because of all the tribes of Israel there were none, except these and Judah, that appeared to pay him this respect. 3. What he did he hastened to do; he lost no time. <hi type="italic">Agree with thy adversary quickly, while thou art in the way.</hi> Here is, (1.) The criminal's submission (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.18-2Sam.19.20">v. 18-20</reference>): <hi type="italic">He fell down before the king,</hi> as a penitent, as a supplicant; and, that he might be thought sincere, he did it publicly before all David's servants, and his friends the men of Judah, yea, and before his own thousand. The offence was public, therefore the submission ought to be so. He owns his crime: <hi type="italic">Thy servant doth know that I have sinned.</hi> He aggravates it: <hi type="italic">I did perversely.</hi> He begs the king's pardon: <hi type="italic">Let not the king impute iniquity to thy servant,</hi> that is, deal with me as I deserve. He intimates that it was below the king's great and generous mind to <hi type="italic">take it to his heart;</hi> and pleads his early return to his allegiance, that he was <hi type="italic">the first of all the house of Joseph</hi> (that is, of Israel, who in the beginning of David's reign had distinguished themselves from Judah by their adherence to Ishbosheth, <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.10">ch. ii. 10</reference>) that came <hi type="italic">to meet the king.</hi> He came first, that by his example of duty the rest might be induced, and by his experience of the king's clemency the rest might be encouraged to follow. (2.) A motion made for judgment against him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">"Shall not Shimei be put to death</hi> as a traitor? Let him, of all men, be made an example." This motion was made by Abishai, who would have ventured his life to have been the death of Shimei when he was cursing, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.9">ch. xvi. 9</reference>. David did not think fit to have it done then, because his judicial power was cut short; but, now that it was restored, why should not the law have its course? Abishai herein consulted what he supposed to be David's feelings more than his true interest. Princes have need to arm themselves against temptations to severity. (3.) His discharge by the king's order, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.22-2Sam.19.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. He rejected Abishai's motion with displeasure: <hi type="italic">What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah?</hi> The less we have to do with those who are of an angry revengeful spirit, and who put us upon doing what is harsh and rigorous, the better. He looks upon these prosecutors as adversaries to him, though they pretended friendship and zeal for his honour. Those who advise us to what is wrong are really <hi type="italic">Satans,</hi> adversaries to us. [1.] They were adversaries to his inclination, which was to clemency. He knew that he was <hi type="italic">this day king in Israel,</hi> restored to, and re-established in, his kingdom, and therefore his honour inclined him to forgive. It is the glory of kings to forgive those that humble and surrender themselves: <hi type="italic">Satis est prostrasse leoni—it suffices the lion that he has laid his victim prostrate.</hi> His joy inclined him to forgive. The pleasantness of his spirit on this great occasion forbade the entrance of any thing that was sour and peevish: joyful days should be forgiving days. Yet this was not all; his experience of God's mercy in restoring him to his kingdom, his exclusion from which he attributed to his sin, inclined him to show mercy to Shimei. Those that are forgiven must forgive. David had severely revenged the abuses done to his ambassadors by the Ammonites (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.31">ch. xii. 31</reference>), but easily passes by the abuse done to himself by an Israelite. That was an affront to Israel in general, and touched the honour of his crown and kingdom; this was purely personal, and therefore (according to the usual disposition of good men) he could the more easily forgive it. [2.] They were adversaries to his interest. If he should put to death Shimei, who cursed him, those would expect the same fate who had taken up arms and actually levied war against him, which would drive them from him, while he was endeavouring to draw them to him. Acts of severity are seldom acts of policy. <hi type="italic">The throne is established by mercy.</hi> Shimei, hereupon, had his pardon signed and sealed with an oath, yet being bound, no doubt, to his good behaviour, and liable to be prosecuted if he afterwards misbehaved; and thus he was reserved to be, in due time, as much a monument of the justice of the government as he was now of its clemency, and in both of its prudence.
entries.e674d7817afcb3620f39199d5cd94714e6840aee: <div eID="gen6362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6363" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> And Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king, and had neither dressed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came <hi type="italic">again</hi> in peace. <hi type="super">25</hi> And it came to pass, when he was come to Jerusalem to meet the king, that the king said unto him, Wherefore wentest not thou with me, Mephibosheth? <hi type="super">26</hi> And he answered, My lord, O king, my servant deceived me: for thy servant said, I will saddle me an ass, that I may ride thereon, and go to the king; because thy servant <hi type="italic">is</hi> lame. <hi type="super">27</hi> And he hath slandered thy servant unto my lord the king; but my lord the king <hi type="italic">is</hi> as an angel of God: do therefore <hi type="italic">what is</hi> good in thine eyes. <hi type="super">28</hi> For all <hi type="italic">of</hi> my father's house were but dead men before my lord the king: yet didst thou set thy servant among them that did eat at thine own table. What right therefore have I yet to cry any more unto the king? <hi type="super">29</hi> And the king said unto him, Why speakest thou any more of thy matters? I have said, Thou and Ziba divide the land. <hi type="super">30</hi> And Mephibosheth said unto the king, Yea, let him take all, forasmuch as my lord the king is come again in peace unto his own house. <div eID="gen6363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6364" type="x-p"/> The day of David's return was a day of bringing to remembrance, a day of account, in which what had passed in his flight was called over again; among other things, after the case of Shimei, that of Mephibosheth comes to be enquired into, and he himself brings it on. <div eID="gen6364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6365" type="x-p"/> I. He went down in the crowd <hi type="italic">to meet the king</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.24">v. 24</reference>), and as a proof of the sincerity of his joy in the king's return, we are here told what a true mourner he was for the king's banishment. During that melancholy time, when one of the greatest glories of Israel had departed, Mephibosheth continued in a very melancholy state. He was never trimmed, nor put on clean linen, but wholly neglected himself, as one abandoned to grief for the king's affliction and the kingdom's misery. In times of public calamity we ought to abridge our enjoyments in the delights of sense, in conformity to the season. There are times when God calls to weeping and mourning, and we must comply with the call. <div eID="gen6365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6366" type="x-p"/> II. When the king came to Jerusalem (since he could not sooner have an opportunity) he made his appearance before him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.25">v. 25</reference>); and when the king asked him why he, being one of his family, had staid behind, and not accompanied him in his exile, he opened his case fully to the king. 1. He complained of Ziba, his servant who should have been his friend, but had been in two ways his enemy; for, first, he had hindered him from going along with the king, by taking the ass himself which he was ordered to make ready for his master (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.26">v. 26</reference>), basely taking advantage of his lameness and his inability to help himself; and, secondly, he had accused him to David of a design to usurp the government, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.27">v. 27</reference>. How much mischief is it in the power of a wicked servant to do to the best master! 2. He gratefully acknowledged the king's great kindness to him when he and all his father's house lay at the king's mercy, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.28">v. 28</reference>. When he might justly have been dealt with as a rebel, he was treated as a friend, as a child: <hi type="italic">Thou didst set thy servant among those that did eat at thy own table.</hi> This shows that Ziba's suggestion was improbable; for could Mephibosheth be so foolish as to aim higher when he lived so easily, so happily as he did? And could he be so very disingenuous as to design any harm to David, of whose great kindness to him he was thus sensible? (3.) He referred his cause to the king's pleasure (<hi type="italic">Do what is good in thy eyes</hi> with me and my estate), depending on the king's wisdom, and his ability to discern between truth and falsehood (<hi type="italic">My lord the king is as an angel from God</hi>), and disclaiming all pretensions of his own merit: "So much kindness I have received above what I deserved, and <hi type="italic">what right have I to cry any more unto the king?</hi> Why should I trouble the king with my complaints when I have already been so troublesome to him? Why should I think any thing hard that is put upon me when I hitherto been so kindly treated?" We were all <hi type="italic">as dead men before God;</hi> yet he has not only spared us, <hi type="italic">but taken us to sit at his table.</hi> How little reason then have we to complain of any trouble we are in, and how much reason to take all well that God does! <div eID="gen6366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6367" type="x-p"/> III. David hereupon recalls the sequestration of Mephibosheth's estate; being deceived in his grant, he revokes it, and confirms his former settlement of it: "<hi type="italic">I have said, Thou and Ziba divide the land</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.29">v. 29</reference>), that is, Let it be as I first ordered it (<reference osisRef="2Sam.9.10">ch. ix. 10</reference>); the property shall still be vested in thee, but Ziba shall have occupancy: he shall till the land, paying thee a rent." Thus Mephibosheth is where he was; no harm is done, only Ziba goes away unpunished for his false and malicious information against his master. David either feared him too much, or loved him too well, to do justice upon him according to that law, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.18-Deut.19.19">Deut. xix. 18, 19</reference>; and he was now in the humour of forgiving and resolved to make every body easy. <div eID="gen6367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6368" type="x-p"/> IV. Mephibosheth drowns all he cares about his estate in his joy for the king's return (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.30">v. 30</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Yea, let him take all,</hi> the presence and favour of the king shall be to me instead of all." A good man can contentedly bear his own private losses and disappointments, while he see Israel in peace, and the throne of the Son of David exalted and established. Let Ziba take all, so that David may be in peace.
entries.73c8b8c6787f8ba3d308cd80e82b19e49d26906d: <div eID="gen6368" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Mephibosheth Meets David. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1023.)</title> <div sID="gen6369" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> And Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim, and went over Jordan with the king, to conduct him over Jordan. <hi type="super">32</hi> Now Barzillai was a very aged man, <hi type="italic">even</hi> fourscore years old: and he had provided the king of sustenance while he lay at Mahanaim; for he <hi type="italic">was</hi> a very great man. <hi type="super">33</hi> And the king said unto Barzillai, Come thou over with me, and I will feed thee with me in Jerusalem. <hi type="super">34</hi> And Barzillai said unto the king, How long have I to live, that I should go up with the king unto Jerusalem? <hi type="super">35</hi> I <hi type="italic">am</hi> this day fourscore years old: <hi type="italic">and</hi> can I discern between good and evil? can thy servant taste what I eat or what I drink? can I hear any more the voice of singing men and singing women? wherefore then should thy servant be yet a burden unto my lord the king? <hi type="super">36</hi> Thy servant will go a little way over Jordan with the king: and why should the king recompense it me with such a reward? <hi type="super">37</hi> Let thy servant, I pray thee, turn back again, that I may die in mine own city, <hi type="italic">and be buried</hi> by the grave of my father and of my mother. But behold thy servant Chimham; let him go over with my lord the king; and do to him what shall seem good unto thee. <hi type="super">38</hi> And the king answered, Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do to him that which shall seem good unto thee: and whatsoever thou shalt require of me, <hi type="italic">that</hi> will I do for thee. <hi type="super">39</hi> And all the people went over Jordan. And when the king was come over, the king kissed Barzillai, and blessed him; and he returned unto his own place. <div eID="gen6369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6370" type="x-p"/> David had already graced the triumphs of his restoration with the generous remission of the injuries that had been done to him; we have him here gracing them with a no less generous reward of the kindnesses that had been shown to him. Barzillai, the Gileadite, who had a noble seat at Rogelim, not far from Mahanaim, was the man who, of all the nobility and gentry of that country, had been most kind to David in his distress. If Absalom had prevailed, it is likely he would have suffered for his loyalty; but now he and his shall be no losers by it. Here is, <div eID="gen6370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6371" type="x-p"/> I. Barzillai's great respect to David, not only as a good man, but as his righteous sovereign: He <hi type="italic">provided him with much sustenance,</hi> for himself and his family, <hi type="italic">while he lay at Mahanaim,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.32">v. 32</reference>. God had given him a large estate, <hi type="italic">for he was a very great man,</hi> and, it seems, he had a large heart to do good with it: what else but that is a large estate good for? To reduced greatness generosity obliges us, and to oppressed goodness piety obliges us, to be in a particular manner kind, to the utmost of our power. Barzillai, to show that he was not weary of David, though he was so great a charge to him, attended him to Jordan, and went over with him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.31">v. 31</reference>. Let subjects learn hence to render <hi type="italic">tribute to whom tribute is due</hi> and <hi type="italic">honour to whom honour,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.13.7">Rom. xiii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen6371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6372" type="x-p"/> II. The kind invitation David gave to him to court (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">Come thou over with me.</hi> He invited him, 1. That he might have the pleasure of his company and the benefit of his counsel; for we may suppose that he was very wise and good, as well as very rich, otherwise he would not have been called here <hi type="italic">a very great man;</hi> for it is what a man is, more than what he has, that renders him truly great. 2. That he might have an opportunity of returning his kindness: "<hi type="italic">I will feed thee with me;</hi> thou shalt fare as sumptuously as I fare, and this at Jerusalem, the royal and holy city." David did not take Barzillai's kindness to him as a debt (he was not one of those arbitrary princes who think that whatever their subjects have is theirs when they please), but accepted it and rewarded it as a favour. We must always study to be grateful to our friends, especially to those who have helped us in distress. <div eID="gen6372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6373" type="x-p"/> III. Barzillai's reply to this invitation, wherein, <div eID="gen6373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6374" type="x-p"/> 1. He admires the king's generosity in making him this offer, lessening his service, and magnifying the king's return for it: <hi type="italic">Why should the king recompense it with such a reward?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.36">v. 36</reference>. Will the master thank that servant who only does what was his duty to do? He though he had done himself honour enough in doing the king any service. Thus, when the saints shall be called to inherit the kingdom in consideration of what they have done for Christ in this world, they will be amazed at the disproportion between the service and the recompence. <reference osisRef="Matt.25.37">Matt. xxv. 37</reference>, <hi type="italic">Lord, when saw we thee hungry, and fed thee?</hi> <div eID="gen6374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6375" type="x-p"/> 2. He declines accepting the invitation. He begs his majesty's pardon for refusing so generous an offer: he should think himself very happy in being near the king, but, (1.) He is old, and unfit to remove at all, especially to court. He is old, and unfit for the <hi type="italic">business</hi> of the court: "Why <hi type="italic">should I go up with the king to Jerusalem?</hi> I can do him no service there, in the council, the camp, the treasury, or the courts of justice; for <hi type="italic">how long have I to live?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.34">v. 34</reference>. Shall I think of going into business, now that I am going out of this world?" He is old and unfit for the <hi type="italic">diversions</hi> of the court, which will be ill-bestowed, and even thrown away, upon one that can relish them so little, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.35">v. 35</reference>. As it was in Moses's time, so it was in Barzillai's and it is not worse now, that, <hi type="italic">if men be so strong that they come to fourscore years, their strength then is labour and sorrow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.90.10">Ps. xc. 10</reference>. These were then, and are still, years of which men say they <hi type="italic">have no pleasure in them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.1">Eccl. xii. 1</reference>. Dainties are insipid when desire fails, and songs to the aged ear are little better than those sung to a heavy heart, very disagreeable: how should they be otherwise when the daughters of music are brought low? Let those that are old learn of Barzillai to be dead to the delights of sense; let grace second nature, and make a virtue of the necessity. Nay, Barzillai, being old, thinks he shall be <hi type="italic">a burden to the king,</hi> rather than any credit to him; and a good man would not go any where to be burdensome, or, if he must be so, will rather be so to his own house than to another's. (2.) He is dying, and must begin to think of his long journey, his removal out of the world, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.37">v. 37</reference>. It is good for us all, but it especially becomes old people to think and speak much of dying. "Talk of going to court!" says Barzillai; "Let me go home and <hi type="italic">die in my own city,</hi> the place of my father's sepulchre; let me die <hi type="italic">by the grave of my father,</hi> that my bones may be quietly carried to the place of their rest. The grave is ready for me, let me go and get ready for it, go and die in my nest." <div eID="gen6375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6376" type="x-p"/> 3. He desires the king to be kind to his son Chimham: <hi type="italic">Let him go over with my lord the king,</hi> and have preferment at court. What favour is done to him Barzillai will take as done to himself. Those that are old must not grudge young people those delights which they themselves are past the enjoyment of, nor confine them to their retirements. Barzillai will go back himself, but he will not make Chimham go back with him; though he could ill spare Chimham, yet, thinking it would gratify and advance him, he is willing to do it. <div eID="gen6376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6377" type="x-p"/> IV. David's farewell to Barzillai. 1. He sends him back into his country with a kiss and a blessing (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.39">v. 39</reference>), signifying that in gratitude for his kindnesses he would love him and pray for him, and with a promise that whatever request he should at any time make to him he would be ready to oblige him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.38">v. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whatsoever thou shalt think of,</hi> when thou comest home, to <hi type="italic">ask of me,</hi> that <hi type="italic">will I do for thee.</hi> What is the chief excellency of power but this, that it gives men a capacity of doing the more good? 2. He takes Chimham forward with him, and leaves it to Barzillai to choose him his preferment. I will <hi type="italic">do to him what shall seem good to thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.38">v. 38</reference>. And, it should seem, Barzillai, who had experienced the innocency and safety of retirement, begged a country seat for him near Jerusalem, but not in it; for, long after, we read of a place near Beth-lehem, David's city, which is called <hi type="italic">the habitation of Chimham,</hi> allotted to him, probably, not out of the crown-lands or the forfeited estates, but out of David's paternal estate.
entries.e05af8c4094e6b09f3e7acfb263b63c68b5c3ca0: <div eID="gen6377" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Quarrel between Israel and Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1023.)</title> <div sID="gen6378" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">40</hi> Then the king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went on with him: and all the people of Judah conducted the king, and also half the people of Israel. <hi type="super">41</hi> And, behold, all the men of Israel came to the king, and said unto the king, Why have our brethren the men of Judah stolen thee away, and have brought the king, and his household, and all David's men with him, over Jordan? <hi type="super">42</hi> And all the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, Because the king <hi type="italic">is</hi> near of kin to us: wherefore then be ye angry for this matter? have we eaten at all of the king's <hi type="italic">cost?</hi> or hath he given us any gift? <hi type="super">43</hi> And the men of Israel answered the men of Judah, and said, We have ten parts in the king, and we have also more <hi type="italic">right</hi> in David than ye: why then did ye despise us, that our advice should not be first had in bringing back our king? And the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel. <div eID="gen6378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6379" type="x-p"/> David came over Jordan attended and assisted only by the men of Judah; but when he had advanced as far as Gilgal, the first stage on this side Jordan, <hi type="italic">half the people of Israel</hi> (that is, of their elders and great men) had come to wait upon him, to kiss his hand, and congratulate him on his return, but found they came too late to witness the solemnity of his first entrance. This put them out of humour, and occasioned a quarrel between them and the men of Judah, which was a damp to the joy of the day, and the beginning of further mischief. Here is, 1. The complaint which the men of Israel brought to the king against the men of Judah (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.41">v. 41</reference>), that they had performed the ceremony of bringing the king over Jordan, and not given them notice, that they might have come to join in it. This reflected upon them, as if they were not so well affected to the king and his restoration as the men of Judah were, whereas the king himself knew that they had spoken of it before the men of Judah thought of it, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.11">v. 11</reference>. It seemed likewise as if they intended to monopolize the king's favours when he had come back, and to be looked upon as his only friends. See what mischief comes from pride and jealousy. 2. The excuse which the men of Judah made for themselves, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.42">v. 42</reference>. (1.) They plead relations to the king: "<hi type="italic">He is near of kin to us,</hi> and therefore in a matter of mere ceremony, as this was, we may claim precedency. It was into our country that he was to be brought, and therefore who so fit as we to bring him?" (2.) They deny the insinuated charge of self-seeking in what they had done: "<hi type="italic">Have we eaten at all of the king's cost?</hi> No, we have all borne our own charges. <hi type="italic">Hath he given us any gift?</hi> No, we have no design to engross the advantages of his return; you have come time enough to share in them." Too many that attend princes do so only for what they can get. 3. The men of Israel's vindication of their charge, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.43">v. 43</reference>. They pleaded, "<hi type="italic">We have ten parts in the king</hi>" (Judah having Simeon only, whose lot lay within his, to join with him), "and therefore it is a slight upon us that our advice was not asked about <hi type="italic">bringing back the king.</hi>" See how uncertain the multitude is. They were lately striving against the king, to drive him out; now they are striving about him, which shall honour him most. A good man and a good cause will thus recover their credit and interest, though, for a time, they may seem to have lost them. See what is commonly the origin of strife, nothing so much as impatience of contempt or the least seeming slight. The men of Judah would have done better if they had taken their brethren's advice and assistance; but, since they did not, why should the men of Israel be so grievously offended? If a good work be done, and well done, let us not be displeased, nor the work disparaged, though we had no hand in it. 4. The scripture takes notice, by way of blame, which of the contending parties managed the cause with most passion: <hi type="italic">The words of the men of Judah were fiercer than</hi> those <hi type="italic">of the men of Israel.</hi> Though we have right and reason on our side, yet, if we express ourselves with fierceness, God takes notice of it and is much displeased with it.  <chapter eID="2Sam.19"/> <div eID="gen6379" type="x-p"/>

entries.b5e2f0e697cc5a32b3b03d62c83f00ceabd56be9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3002"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 19</title> <div sID="gen4153" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.1-2Sam.19.8">2Sa 19:1-8</reference>. Joab Causes the King to Cease Mourning.<div eID="gen4153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4154" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3002"/><hi type="bold">3. the people gat them by stealth ... to the city--</hi>The rumor of the king's disconsolate condition spread a universal and unseasonable gloom. His troops, instead of being welcomed back (as a victorious army always was) with music and other demonstrations of public joy, slunk secretly and silently into the city, as if ashamed after the commission of some crime. <div eID="gen4154" type="x-p"/>
entries.7cfeeb3c00e7de610528c52f22993bd81692cc80: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3003"/><div sID="gen4155" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3003"/><hi type="bold">4. the king covered his face--</hi>one of the usual signs of mourning (see on <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>). <div eID="gen4155" type="x-p"/>
entries.85e217832ec2ab9725dbe7ed10d1eb4cf6041781: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3004"/><div sID="gen4156" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3004"/><hi type="bold">5. Thou hast shamed ... the faces of all thy servants--</hi>by withdrawing thyself to indulge in grief, as if their services were disagreeable and their devotion irksome to thee. Instead of hailing their return with joy and gratitude, thou hast refused them the small gratification of seeing thee. Joab's remonstrance was right and necessary, but it was made with harshness. He was one of those persons who spoil their important services by the insolence of their manners, and who always awaken a feeling of obligation in those to whom they render any services. He spoke to David in a tone of hauteur that ill became a subject to show towards his king. <div eID="gen4156" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8037211a9c1f890903961903ff144e86598b517: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3005"/><div sID="gen4157" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3005"/><hi type="bold">7. Now ... arise, go forth, and speak comfortably unto thy servants--</hi>The king felt the truth of Joab's reprimand; but the threat by which it was enforced, grounded as it was on the general's unbounded popularity with the army, showed him to be a dangerous person; and that circumstance, together with the violation of an express order to deal gently for his sake with Absalom, produced in David's mind a settled hatred, which was strongly manifested in his last directions to Solomon. <div eID="gen4157" type="x-p"/>
entries.62c653cb27479b5b84df4a75b3b469c223d76b13: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3006"/><div sID="gen4158" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3006"/><hi type="bold">8. the king arose, and sat in the gate--</hi>He appeared daily in the usual place for the hearing of causes.<div eID="gen4158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all the people came before the king--</hi>that is, the loyal natives who had been faithful to his government, and fought in his cause.<div eID="gen4159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4160" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Israel had fled--</hi>that is, the adherents of Absalom, who, on his defeat, had dispersed and saved themselves by flight.<div eID="gen4160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4161" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.9-2Sam.19.43">2Sa 19:9-43</reference>. The Israelites Bring the King Back. <div eID="gen4161" type="x-p"/>
entries.cdac15615a03572a168c7999b7d4958092f9fe30: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3007"/><div sID="gen4162" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3007"/><hi type="bold">9-11. all the people were at strife throughout all the tribes of Israel--</hi>The kingdom was completely disorganized. The sentiments of three different parties are represented in <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.9">2Sa 19:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.10">10</reference>: the royalists, the adherents of Absalom who had been very numerous, and those who were indifferent to the Davidic dynasty. In these circumstances the king was right in not hastening back, as a conqueror, to reascend his throne. A re-election was, in some measure, necessary. He remained for some time on the other side of Jordan, in expectation of being invited back. That invitation was given without, however, the concurrence of Judah. David, disappointed and vexed by his own tribe's apparent lukewarmness, despatched the two high priests to rouse the Judahites to take a prominent interest in his cause. It was the act of a skilful politician. Hebron having been the seat of the rebellion, it was graceful on his part to encourage their return to allegiance and duty; it was an appeal to their honor not to be the last of the tribes. But this separate message, and the preference given to them, occasioned an outburst of jealousy among the other tribes that was nearly followed by fatal consequences [see <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.40">2Sa 19:40</reference>-43]. <div eID="gen4162" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1d7a346e2dd1191fcb90ccfff5b31398b37fcd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3008"/><div sID="gen4163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3008"/><hi type="bold">13. And say ye to Amasa, &c.--</hi>This also was a dextrous stroke of policy. David was fully alive to the importance, for extinguishing the rebellion, of withdrawing from that cause the only leader who could keep it alive; and he, therefore, secretly intimated his intention to raise Amasa to the command of the army in the place of Joab, whose overbearing haughtiness had become intolerable. The king justly reckoned, that from natural temper as well as gratitude for the royal pardon, he would prove a more tractable servant; and David, doubtless, intended in all sincerity to fulfil this promise. But Joab managed to retain his high position (see on <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.4-2Sam.20.10">2Sa 20:4-10</reference>). <div eID="gen4163" type="x-p"/>
entries.8201b1676098950b189061cfa5f89056aef1f548: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3009"/><div sID="gen4164" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3009"/><hi type="bold">14. he bowed the heart of all the men of Judah--</hi>that is, Amasa, who had been won over, used his great influence in re-attaching the whole tribe of Judah to the interest of David. <div eID="gen4164" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5e1bf72503a7fdaf2368066f89d40c23f27ab80: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3010"/><div sID="gen4165" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3010"/><hi type="bold">15. Judah came to Gilgal--</hi>the most convenient place where preparations could be made for bringing the king and court over the Jordan. <div eID="gen4165" type="x-p"/>
entries.6baddec5571fc33d716417621f1cc520293285ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3011"/><div sID="gen4166" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3011"/><hi type="bold">16-23. Shemei ... a thousand men of Benjamin with him--</hi>This display of [Shemei's] followers was to show what force he could raise against or in support of the king. Expressing the deepest regret for his former outrageous conduct, he was pardoned on the spot; and although the son of Zeruiah urged the expediency of making this chief a public example, his officiousness was repulsed by David with magnanimity, and with the greater confidence that he felt himself now re-established in the kingdom (see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.8">1Ki 2:8</reference>). <div eID="gen4166" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb45331839971c0c9660a22ec8a9d4dfaa6a3e5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3015"/><div sID="gen4170" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3015"/><hi type="bold">24-30. Mephibosheth ... came down to meet the king--</hi>The reception given to Mephibosheth was less creditable to David. The sincerity of that prince's grief for the misfortunes of the king cannot be doubted.<div eID="gen4170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">He had neither dressed his feet--</hi>not taken the bath,<div eID="gen4171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4172" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor trimmed his beard--</hi>The Hebrews cut off the hair on the upper lip (see on <reference osisRef="Lev.13.45">Le 13:45</reference>), and cheeks, but carefully cherished it on the chin from ear to ear. Besides dyeing it black or red colors, which, however, is the exception, and not the rule in the East, there are various modes of trimming it: they train it into a massy, bushy form, swelling and round; or they terminate it like a pyramid, in a sharp point. Whatever the mode, it is always trimmed with the greatest care; and they usually carry a small comb for the purpose. The neglect of this attention to his beard was an undoubted proof of the depth of Mephibosheth's grief. The king seems to have received him upbraidingly, and not to have been altogether sure either of his guilt or innocence. It is impossible to commend the cavalier treatment, any more than to approve the partial award, of David in this case. If he were too hurried and distracted by the pressure of circumstances to inquire fully into the matter, he should have postponed his decision; for if by "dividing the land" (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.29">2Sa 19:29</reference>) he meant that the former arrangement should be continued by which Mephibosheth was acknowledged the proprietor, and Ziba the farmer, it was a hardship inflicted on the owner to fix him with a tenant who had so grossly slandered him. But if by "dividing the land," they were now to share alike, the injustice of the decision was greatly increased. In any view, the generous, disinterested spirit displayed by Mephibosheth was worthy a son of the noble-hearted Jonathan. <div eID="gen4172" type="x-p"/>
entries.026130efc236c5a61a6b5be3a823d1c8770d97ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3016"/><div sID="gen4173" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3016"/><hi type="bold">31-40. Barzillai the Gileadite--</hi>The rank, great age, and chivalrous devotion of this Gileadite chief wins our respect. His declining to go to court, his recommendation of his son, his convoy across the Jordan, and his parting scene with the king, are interesting incidents. What mark of royal favor was bestowed on Chimham has not been recorded; but it is probable that David gave a great part of his personal patrimony in Beth-lehem to Chimham and his heirs in perpetuity (<reference osisRef="Jer.41.17">Jr 41:17</reference>). <div eID="gen4173" type="x-p"/>

entries.9b7ac812cc69c9ce3769dd65599e95751bba7477: <div eID="gen11213" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen11214" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11215" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11215" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11214" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11216" type="x-p"/> David continues his lamentation for his son, and the people are greatly discouraged, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.1-2Sam.19.4">2Sam 19:1-4</reference>. Joab reproves and threatens him with the general defection of the people, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.5-2Sam.19.7">2Sam 19:5-7</reference>. David lays aside his mourning, and shows himself to the people, who are thereby encouraged, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.8">2Sam 19:8</reference>. The tribes take counsel to bring the king back to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.9-2Sam.19.12">2Sam 19:9-12</reference>. He makes Amasa captain of the host in place of Joab, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.13">2Sam 19:13</reference>. The king, returning, is met by Judah at Gilgal, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.14">2Sam 19:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.15">2Sam 19:15</reference>. Shimei comes to meet David, and entreats for his life, which David grants, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.16-2Sam.19.23">2Sam 19:16-23</reference>. Mephibosheth also meets him, and shows how he had been slandered by Ziba, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.24-2Sam.19.30">2Sam 19:24-30</reference>. David is met by Barzillai, and between them there is an affecting interview, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.31-2Sam.19.40">2Sam 19:31-40</reference>. Contention between the men of Judah and the men of Israel, about bringing back the king, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.41-2Sam.19.43">2Sam 19:41-43</reference>.
entries.28eee46af66a6c6654a00e3bf96062d234bb3857: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen11216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11217" type="x-p"/> The victory - was turned into mourning - Instead of rejoicing that a most unnatural and ruinous rebellion had been quashed, the people mourned over their own success, because they saw their king so immoderately afflicted for the loss of his worthless son.
entries.cab91829b0a7dfe032f44f4110f631a70682a3c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen11217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11218" type="x-p"/> The king covered his face - This was the custom of mourners. <div eID="gen11218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11219" type="x-p"/> O my son Absalom - Calmet has properly remarked that the frequent repetition of the name of the defunct, is common in the language of lamentation. Thus Virgil, act. v., ver. 51: - - Daphnin que team tollemus ad astra; <div eID="gen11219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11220" type="x-p"/> Daphnin ad astra feremus: amavit nos quoque Daphnis. "With yours, my song I cheerfully shall join, <div eID="gen11220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11221" type="x-p"/> To raise your Daphnis to the powers Divine. <div eID="gen11221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11222" type="x-p"/> Daphnis I'll raise unto the powers above, <div eID="gen11222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11223" type="x-p"/> For dear to me was Daphnis' well tried love." <div eID="gen11223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11224" type="x-p"/> See the notes on the preceding chapter, 2 Samuel 18 (note).
entries.9bb7c6f405b7c6f8bc2c78c93c95ee5953ff21d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen11224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11225" type="x-p"/> Thou hast shamed this day - Joab's speech to David on his immoderate grief for the death of his rebellious son is not only remarkable for the insolence of office, but also for good sense and firmness. Every man who candidly considers the state of the case, must allow that David acted imprudently at least; and that Joab's firm reproof was necessary to arouse him to a sense of his duty to his people. But still, in his manner, Joab had far exceeded the bonds of that reverence which a servant owes to his master, or a subject to his prince. Joab was a good soldier, but in every respect a bad man, and a dangerous subject.
entries.37dc3c63bedaf333378d2230387f72d2320dde42: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen11225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11226" type="x-p"/> The king - sat in the gate - The place where justice was administered to the people.
entries.048a03bdab99bca47f5ec1fd02ed5738af4bbdbf: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen11226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11227" type="x-p"/> Speak unto the elders of Judah - David was afraid to fall out with this tribe: they were in possession of Jerusalem, and this was a city of great importance to him. They had joined Absalom in his rebellion; and doubtless were now ashamed of their conduct. David appears to take no notice of their infidelity, but rather to place confidence in them, that their confidence in him might be naturally excited: and, to oblige them yet farther, purposes to make Amasa captain of the host in the place of Joab.
entries.655be8c35d8c5dd39c591fe2256aca634d63e1b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen11227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11228" type="x-p"/> And he bowed the heart of all the men of Judah - The measures that he pursued were the best calculated that could be to accomplish this salutary end. Appear to distrust those whom you have some reason to suspect, and you increase their caution and distrust. Put as much confidence in them as you safely can, and this will not fail to excite their confidence towards you.
entries.e82113becc685fb02b6776b65b622b964ca481e4: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen11228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11229" type="x-p"/> Shimei the son of Gera - It appears that Shimei was a powerful chieftain in the land; for he had here, in his retinue, no less than a thousand men.
entries.660265c0945afd39deaa03c74dcb747de6e7ed63: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen11229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11230" type="x-p"/> There went over a ferry-boat - This is the first mention of any thing of the kind. Some think a bridge or raft is what is here intended.
entries.d1f7db5925e1b73c15f019be171fc66f3b2b836c: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen11230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11231" type="x-p"/> For thy servant doth know that I have sinned - This was all he could do; his subsequent conduct alone could prove his sincerity. On such an avowal as this David could not but grant him his life.
entries.8c15d5791a94093c15cfdd157a10f4f1a59b0c25: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen11231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11232" type="x-p"/> Neither dressed his feet - He had given the fullest proof of his sincere attachment to David and his cause; and by what he had done, amply refuted the calumnies of his servant Ziba.
entries.d67407d80413339ba4114b9105c7888ba0e7c883: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen11232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11233" type="x-p"/> The king is as an angel of God - As if he had said, I state my case plainly and without guile; thou art too wise not to penetrate the motives from which both myself and servant have acted. I shall make no appeal; with whatsoever thou determinest I shall rest contented.
entries.06bf4e5ae46ba9d35018ed42cf444d7f88378867: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen11233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11234" type="x-p"/> I have said, Thou and Ziba divide the land - At first, David gave the land of Saul to Mephibosheth; and Ziba, his sons, and his servants, were to work that land; and to Mephibosheth, as the lord, he was to give the half of the produce. Ziba met David in his distress with provisions, and calumniated Mephibosheth: David, too slightly trusting to his misrepresentation, and supposing that Mephibosheth was actually such a traitor as Ziba represented him, made him on the spot a grant of his master's land. Now he finds that he has acted too rashly, and therefore confirms the former grant; i.e. that Ziba should cultivate the ground, and still continue to give to Mephibosheth, as the lord, the half of the produce. This was merely placing things in statu quo, and utterly annulling the gift that he had made to Ziba. But why did he leave this treacherous man any thing? Answer, <div eID="gen11234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11235" type="x-p"/> 1. He was one of the domestics of Saul, and David wished to show kindness to that house. <div eID="gen11235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11236" type="x-p"/> 2. He had supplied him with the necessaries of life when he was in the greatest distress; and he thinks proper to continue him in his old office, by way of remuneration. <div eID="gen11236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11237" type="x-p"/> But it was certainly too great a compensation for his services, however then important, when all the circumstances are considered.
entries.e29cdd5509998a81228f6c7fd991b159598a8e58: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen11237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11238" type="x-p"/> Barzillai was a very aged man - This venerable person had given full proof of his attachment to David by the supplies he had given him when he lay at Mahanaim, where his case was all but desperate; the sincerity of his congratulations now none can suspect. David's offer to him was at once noble and liberal: he wished to compensate such a man, and he wished to have at hand such a friend.
entries.28e31ff819f69e72caf70ef091e5a57a41504f7c: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen11238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11239" type="x-p"/> Can thy servant taste what I eat - Here is at once an affecting description of the infirmities of old age; and a correct account of the mode of living at an Eastern court in ancient times. <div eID="gen11239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11240" type="x-p"/> Barzillai was fourscore years old; his ear was become dull of hearing, and his relish for his food was gone: he therefore appears to have been not only an old man, but an infirm old man. Besides delicate meats and drinks, we find that vocal music constituted a principal part of court entertainments: male and female singers made a necessary appendage to these banquets, as they do in most Eastern courts to the present day. As David was a most sublime poet, and emphatically styled the sweet singer of Israel, he no doubt had his court well supplied with vocal as well as instrumental performers; and, probably, with poets and poetesses; for it is not likely that he was the only poet of his time, though he undoubtedly was the most excellent.
entries.9fd5af29eb0b7bda956645f760e41d3d851c0883: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen11240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11241" type="x-p"/> Thy servant Chimham - It is generally understood that this was Barzillai's son; and this is probable from <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.7">1Kgs 2:7</reference>, where, when David was dying, he said, Show kindness to the sons of Barzillai: and it is very probable that this Chimham was one of them. In <reference osisRef="Jer.41.17">Jer 41:17</reference> mention is made of the habitation of Chimham, which was near to Bethlehem; and it is reasonably conjectured that David had left that portion, which was probably a part of his paternal estate, to this son of Barzillai.
entries.c6d021b52589a8a618b05e349109041e8f7f728d: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen11241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11242" type="x-p"/> The king kissed Barzillai, and blessed him - The kiss was the token of friendship and farewell; the blessing was a prayer to God for his prosperity, probably a prophetical benediction.
entries.07c92cad25d5cfd2f088d3f022cbaf626665ae9e: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen11242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11243" type="x-p"/> Wherefore then be ye angry for this matter? - We have not done this for our own advantage; we have gained nothing by it; we did it through loyal attachment to our king.
entries.9212e2f17ce134a7501e8e0d8ca2c8e34e635dc6: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen11243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11244" type="x-p"/> We have ten parts in the king, and - more right - We are ten tribes to one, or we are ten times so many as you; and consequently should have been consulted in this business. <div eID="gen11244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11245" type="x-p"/> The words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel - They had more weight, for they had more reason on their side. <div eID="gen11245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11246" type="x-p"/> It is pleasant when every province, canton, district, and county, vie with each other in personal attachment to the prince, and loyal attachment to his government. From such contentions as these civil wars are never likely to arise. And how blessed it must be for the country where the king merits all this! where the prince is the pastor and father of his people, and in all things the minister of and to them for good! <div eID="gen11246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11247" type="x-p"/> It is criminal in the prince not to endeavor to deserve the confidence and love of his people; and it is highly criminal in the people not to repay such endeavors with the most loyal and affectionate attachment. <div eID="gen11247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11248" type="x-p"/> Where the government is not despotic, the king acts by the counsels of his ministers, and while he does so he is not chargeable with miscarriages and misfortunes; they either came through bad counsels, or directly thwarting providences. On this ground is that political maxim in our laws formed, the king can do no wrong. Sometimes God will have things otherwise than the best counsels have determined, because he sees that the results will, on the whole, be better for the peace and prosperity of that state. "God is the only Ruler of princes." And as the peace of the world depends much on civil government, hence kings and civil governors are peculiar objects of the Almighty's care. Wo to him who labors to bring about a general disaffection; as such things almost invariably end in general disappointment and calamity. It is much easier to unsettle than to settle; to pull down than to build up.  <chapter eID="2Sam.19"/> <div eID="gen11248" type="x-p"/>

entries.ce5ecbf19abc271538a2493fc34f7bcd72130839: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.1-2Sam.19.3">2Sa 19:1-3</reference> <hi type="italic">David’s mourning, and Joab’s reproof.</hi> - <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.1">2Sa 19:1</reference>-6. When Joab was told that the king was mourning and weeping for Absalom, he went to him into the house to expostulate with him. <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.5">2Sa 19:5</reference> introduces the continuation of <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.1">2Sa 19:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.2-2Sam.19.4">2Sa 19:2-4</reference> contain parenthetical sentences, describing the impression made upon the people by the king’s mourning. Through the king’s deep trouble, the salvation (the victory) upon that day became mourning for all the people who had fought for David, and they went by stealth in to the city (לבוא יתגּנּב: they stole to come, came by stealth), “as people steal away who have covered themselves with shame, when they flee in battle.”
entries.76559f6ea2a7af79827a2cb79bea87e6db89399c: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.4">2Sa 19:4</reference> <div eID="gen4517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4518" type="x-p"/> But the king had covered his face, and cried aloud, “My son Absalom,” etc.
entries.2f1f3588c14d37821fbf0499361788c5be3ce613: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.5">2Sa 19:5</reference> <div eID="gen4518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4519" type="x-p"/> Then Joab went into the house to the king, and said to him, “Thou hast shamed this day the faces of all thy servants who have saved thy life, and the life of thy sons and daughters, thy wives and concubines” (covered them with shame, by deceiving their hope that thou wouldest rejoice in the victory).
entries.919a52822f0bf0749014c65f85aa2a51b93c24df: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.6">2Sa 19:6</reference> לאהבה, “to love” (i.e., in that thou lovest) “those who hate thee, and hatest those who love thee; for thou hast given to know to-day (through thy conduct) that chiefs and servants (commanders and soldiers) are nothing (are worth nothing); for I have perceived to-day (or I perceive to-day) that if (לא for לוּ) Absalom were alive, and we had all perished, that it would be right in thine eyes.”
entries.f910129c65e9d35eb2a2b388f6c2d1da90c602d9: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.7">2Sa 19:7</reference> “And now rise up, go out and speak to the heart of thy servants (i.e., speak to them in a friendly manner: <reference osisRef="Gen.34.3">Gen 34:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.50.21">Gen 50:21</reference>, etc.): for I swear by Jehovah, if thou go not out, verily not a man will stay with thee to-night; and this will be worse to thee than all the evil that has come upon thee from thy youth until now.” Joab was certainly not only justified, but bound in David’s own interests, to expostulate with him upon his conduct, and to urge him to speak in a friendly manner to the people who had exposed their lives for him, inasmuch as his present conduct would necessarily stifle the affection of the people towards their king, and might be followed by the most serious results with reference to his throne. At the same time, he did this in so heartless and lordly a manner, that the king could not fail to be deeply hurt by his words.
entries.aaeee2dd1a3678023e302a38e9d46d93cef7ef1b: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.8">2Sa 19:8</reference> <div eID="gen4519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4520" type="x-p"/> Nevertheless David was obliged to yield to his representations. <hi type="italic">“The king rose up, and sat in the gate, and ... all the people came before the king,”</hi> i.e., the troops marched before the king, who (as we may supply from the context) manifested his good-will in both looks and words. But Israel, i.e., that portion of the people which had followed Absalom, had returned to its tents (i.e., gone home: cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.17">2Sa 18:17</reference>). This sentence forms the transition to the account which follows.
entries.e66a1a09e2e3f8c8a45b9fd90b1a0b6a4f43436e: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.9-2Sam.19.10">2Sa 19:9-10</reference> <hi type="italic">Preliminaries to the return of David to Jerusalem.</hi> - <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.9">2Sa 19:9</reference>, 2Sa 19:10.
