As the rebellion was entirely crushed by Absalom’s death, and the dispersion of his followers to their respective homes, there arose a movement among all the tribes in favour of David. “All the people were disputing (נדון, casting reproaches at one another) in all the tribes of Israel, saying, The king has saved us out of the hand of our enemies, ... and now he is fled out of the land before Absalom. But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, is dead in battle; and now why do ye keep still, to bring back the king?” This movement arose from the consciousness of having done an injustice to the king, in rising up in support of Absalom.
entries.885a406a4eab50439137583ab1035aa53ba085af: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.11-2Sam.19.12">2Sa 19:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen4520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4521" type="x-p"/> When these words of all Israel were reported to David, he sent to the priests Zadok and Abiathar, saying, “Speak to the elders of Judah, why will ye be the last to bring back the king to his palace? ... Ye are my brethren, my bones and flesh (i.e., my blood relations): why then,” etc.? The last clause of <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.11">2Sa 19:11</reference>, <hi type="italic">“the speech of all Israel is come to the king, even to his house,”</hi> is a circumstantial clause inserted in the midst of David’s words, to explain the appeal to the men of Judah not to be the last. In the lxx, and some Codices of the Vulgate, this sentence occurs twice, viz., at the end of <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.10">2Sa 19:10</reference>, and also of <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.11">2Sa 19:11</reference>; and Thenius, Ewald, and Böttcher regard the clause at the end of <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.10">2Sa 19:10</reference> as the original one, and the repetition of it at the close of <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.11">2Sa 19:11</reference> as a gloss. But this is certainly a mistake: for if the clause, “and the speech of all Israel came to the king to his house (at Mahanaim),” ought to stand at the close of <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.10">2Sa 19:10</reference>, and assigns the reason for David’s sending to Zadok and Abiathar, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.11">2Sa 19:11</reference> would certainly, or rather necessarily, commence with המּלך ויּשׁלח: “The word of all Israel came to the king, and then king David sent,” etc. But instead of this, it commences with שׁלח דּיד והמּלך, “But king David sent.” This construction of the sentence decidedly favour the correctness of the Hebrew text; whereas the text of the Septuagint, apart altogether from the tautological repetition of the whole of the sentence in question, shows obviously enough that it is nothing more than a conjecture, by which the attempt was made to remove the difficulty occasioned by the striking position in which the circumstantial clause occurred.
entries.81d87a4b52f757e83c53d156da662b088648d196: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.13">2Sa 19:13</reference> “And say ye to Amasa, Art thou not my bone and flesh? so shall God do to me, and so add, if thou shalt not be prince of the army (chief captain) before me continually in the place of Joab.”
entries.113ac14bca23b9cb721b6f04bbfc9338e308756d: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.14">2Sa 19:14</reference> <div eID="gen4521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4522" type="x-p"/> Thus he (David) inclined the heart of all the people as of one man, and they sent to the king, saying, “Return thou, with all thy servants.” The result of David’s message to the priests is given summarily here. The subject to ויּט is David, not Amasa or Zadok. So far as the fact itself is concerned, it was certainly wise of David to send to the members of his own tribe, and appeal to them not to be behind the rest of the tribes in taking part in his restoration to the kingdom, lest it should appear as though the tribe of Judah, to which David himself belonged, was dissatisfied with his victory, since it was in that tribe that the rebellion itself first broke out; and this would inevitably feed the jealousy between Judah and the rest of the tribes. But it was not only unwise, but unjust, to give to Amasa, the traitor-general of the rebels, a promise on oath that he should be commander-in-chief in the place of Joab; for even if the promise was only given privately at first, the fact that it had been given could not remain a secret from Joab very long, and would be sure to stir up his ambition, and lead him to the commission of fresh crimes, and in all probability the enmity of this powerful general would become dangerous to the throne of David. For however Joab might have excited David’s anger by slaying Absalom, and by the offensive manner in which he had reproved the king for giving way to his grief, David ought to have suppressed his anger in his existing circumstances, and ought not to have rendered evil for evil, especially as he was not only about to pardon Amasa’s crime, but even to reward him as one of his faithful servants.
entries.66519ffe88c32bd3defef67f56e6c9b7d947392d: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.15-2Sam.19.16">2Sa 19:15-16</reference> <hi type="italic">Return of the king; and occurrences at the crossing of the Jordan.</hi> - <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.15">2Sa 19:15</reference>-23. <hi type="italic">Pardon of Shimei.</hi> - <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.15">2Sa 19:15</reference>, 2Sa 19:16. When David reached the Jordan on his return, and Judah had come to Gilgal “to meet him, to conduct the king over the Jordan,” i.e., to form an escort at the crossing, Shimei the Benjaminite hastened down from Bahurim (see 2Sa 16:5.) with the men of Judah to meet David.
entries.3d18a7bf999de5aaace75e72d2a9c9b9c5c158ac: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.17-2Sam.19.19">2Sa 19:17-19</reference> <div eID="gen4522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4523" type="x-p"/> There also came along with Shimei a thousand men of Benjamin, and Ziba the servant of the house of Saul, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants (see <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.10">2Sa 9:10</reference>); and they went over the Jordan before the king, viz., through a ford, and the ferry-boat had crossed over to carry over the king’s family, and to do whatever seemed good to him, i.e., to be placed at the king’s sole disposal. And Shimei fell down before the king, בּעברו, i.e., <hi type="italic">“when he</hi> (David) <hi type="italic">was about to cross over the Jordan,”</hi> not “when Shimei had crossed over the Jordan;” for after what has just been stated, such a remark would be superfluous: moreover, it is very doubtful whether the infinitive with בּ can express the sense of the pluperfect. Shimei said, “Let not my lord impute to me any crime, and do not remember how thy servant hath sinned.”
entries.9b52f3eb0c8f0ccd8a27e3f1099e4992ae2e53fa: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.20-2Sam.19.23">2Sa 19:20-23</reference> “For thy servant knoweth (i.e., I know) that I have sinned, and behold I have come to-day the first of the whole house of Joseph, to go to meet my lord the king.” By <hi type="italic">“the whole house of Joseph”</hi> we are to understand the rest of the tribes with the exception of Judah, who are called <hi type="italic">“all Israel”</hi> in 2Sa 19:12. There is no reason for the objection taken by Thenius and Böttcher to the expression בּית־יוסף. This rendering of the lxx (παντὸς Ἰσραὴλ καὶ οἴκου Ἰωσήφ) does not prove that כּלישׂראל was the original reading, but only that the translator thought it necessary to explain οἴκου Ἰωσήφ by adding the gloss παντὸς Ἰσραὴλ; and the assertion that it was only in the oratorical style of a later period, when the kingdom had been divided, that Joseph became the party name of all that were not included in Judah, is overthrown by 1Ki 11:28. The designation of the tribes that opposed Judah by the name of the leading tribe (<hi type="italic">Joseph</hi>: <reference osisRef="Josh.16.1">Jos 16:1</reference>) was as old as the jealousy between these tribes and Judah, which did not commence with the division of the kingdom, but was simply confirmed thereby into a permanent distinction. Shimei’s prayer for the forgiveness of his sin was no more a proof of sincere repentance than the reason which he adduced in support of his petition, namely that he was the first of all the house of Joseph to come and meet David. Shimei’s only desire was to secure impunity for himself. Abishai therefore replied (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.21">2Sa 19:21</reference>), “Shall not Shimei be put to death for this (זאת תּחת, for this, which he has just said and done), because he hath cursed the anointed of Jehovah?” (vid., 2Sa 16:5.). But David answered (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.22">2Sa 19:22</reference>), “What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.10">2Sa 16:10</reference>), for ye become opponents to me to-day?” שׂטן, <hi type="italic">an opponent</hi>, who places obstacles in the way (Num 22:22); here it signifies one who would draw away to evil. “Should any one be put to death in Israel to-day? for do I not know that I am this day king over Israel?” The reason assigned by David here for not punishing the blasphemer as he had deserved, by taking away his life, would have been a very laudable one if the king had really forgiven him. But as David when upon his deathbed charged his successor to punish Shimei for this cursing (1Ki 2:8-9), the favour shown him here was only a sign of David’s weakness, which was not worthy of imitation, the more especially as the king swore unto him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.24">2Sa 19:24</reference>) that he should not die.<hi type="italic">David’s conduct towards Mephibosheth admits</hi> still less of justification.
entries.e1adad5be55c6a6532cd0db4fc2b88ac77ac00a4: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.24">2Sa 19:24</reference> <div eID="gen4523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4524" type="x-p"/> Mephibosheth, the son, i.e., grandson, of Saul, had also come down (from Jerusalem to the Jordan) to meet David, and had not <hi type="italic">“made his feet and his beard,”</hi> i.e., had not washed his feet or arranged his beard (עשׂה, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.21.12">Deu 21:12</reference>), and had not washed his clothes - all of them signs of deep mourning (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.17">Eze 24:17</reference>) - since the day that the king had gone (i.e., had fled from Jerusalem) until the day that he came (again) in peace.
entries.8e9d1b1de08ed9bf96b51c9ed9b0dd0f9171b914: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.25">2Sa 19:25</reference> <hi type="italic">“Now when Jerusalem</hi> (i.e., the inhabitants of the capital) <hi type="italic">came to meet the king,”</hi><note placement="foot">Dathe and Thenius propose to alter ירוּשׁלים into מירוּשׁלים (<hi type="italic">from</hi> Jerusalem), from a simple misunderstanding of the true meaning of the words; for, as Böttcher has observed, the latter (<hi type="italic">from</hi> Jerusalem) would be quite superfluous, as it is already contained in the previous ירד. But Böttcher’s emendation of בּא into בּאה, because Jerusalem or the population of Jerusalem is a feminine notion, is equally unnecessary, since towns and lands are frequently construed as masculines when the inhabitants are intended (vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §318, a.). On the other hand, the rendering adopted by the lxx, and by Luther, Michaelis, and Maurer, in which ירוּשׁלים is taken as an accusative in the sense of “when Mephibosheth came to Jerusalem to meet the king,” is altogether wrong, and has been very properly given up by modern expositors, inasmuch as it is at variance not only with the word ירד, but also with <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.3">2Sa 16:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.13">2Sa 9:13</reference>, where Mephibosheth is said to have lived in Jerusalem.</note> <div eID="gen4524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4525" type="x-p"/> David said to him (i.e., to Mephibosheth, who was with the deputation from the capital which welcomed David at the Jordan), <hi type="italic">“Why wentest thou not with me, Mephibosheth?”</hi> David was justified in putting this question after what Ziba had told him concerning Mephibosheth (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.3">2Sa 16:3</reference>).
entries.c3ffe3cac2d3784cb913bc815bf6a627952507d7: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.26">2Sa 19:26</reference> <div eID="gen4525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4526" type="x-p"/> Mephibosheth replied, “My lord king, my servant hath deceived me: for thy servant thought I will have the ass saddled and go to the king; for thy servant is lame.” If we understand אחבּשׁד as signifying that Mephibosheth had the ass saddled by a servant, and not that he saddled it with his own hands, the meaning is obvious, and there is no ground whatever for altering the text. חבשׁ is certainly used in this sense in <reference osisRef="Gen.22.3">Gen 22:3</reference>, and it is very common for things to be said to be done by a person, even though not done with his own hands. The rendering adopted by the lxx and Vulgate, “Thy servant said to him (the servant), Saddle me the ass,” is not true to the words, though correct so far as the sense is concerned.
entries.5aca81d1b3419e3808f9c8eca19e68945c1973ab: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.27-2Sam.19.30">2Sa 19:27-30</reference> “And he (Ziba) slandered thy servant to my lord the king.” Mephibosheth had not merely inferred this from David’s words, and the tone in which they were spoken, but had certainly found it out long ago, since Ziba would not delay very long to put David’s assurance, that all the possessions of Mephibosheth should belong to him, in force against his master, so that Mephibosheth would discover from that how Ziba had slandered him. “And my lord the king is as the angel of God,” i.e., he sees all just as it really is (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.17">2Sa 14:17</reference>); “and do what is good in thy sight: for all my father’s house (the whole of my family) were but men of death against my lord the king (i.e., thou mightest have had us all put to death), and thou didst set thy servant among thy companions at table (see <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.7">2Sa 9:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.11">2Sa 9:11</reference>); and what right or (what) more have I still to cry (for help) to the king?” The meaning is, “I cannot assert any claims, but will yield to anything you decide concerning me.” It must have been very evident to David from these words of Mephibosheth, that he had been deceived by Ziba, and that he had formed an unfounded prejudice against Mephibosheth, and committed an act of injustice in handing over his property to Ziba. He therefore replied, in evident displeasure (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.29">2Sa 19:29</reference>), “Why talkest thou still of thine affairs? I have said, thou and Ziba shall divide the field?” to which Mephibosheth answered (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.30">2Sa 19:30</reference>), “He may take the whole, since my lord the king has returned in peace to his own house.” This reply shows very clearly that an injustice had been done to Mephibosheth, even if it is not regarded as an expression of wounded feeling on the part of Mephibosheth because of David’s words, but, according to the view taken by Seb. Schmidt and others, as a vindication of himself, as said not to blame the king for the opinion he had formed, but simply to defend himself. But this completely overthrows the opinion held by Thenius and O. v. Gerlach, that David’s words in <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.30">2Sa 19:30</reference> contain nothing more than a revocation of his hasty declaration in <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.4">2Sa 16:4</reference>, and a confirmation of his first decision in <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.7-2Sam.9.10">2Sa 9:7-10</reference>, and are to be understood as signifying, “Let everything be as I settled it at first; hold the property jointly,” inasmuch as Ziba and his sons had of course obtained their living from the produce of the land. Moreover, the words “thou and Ziba divide the land” are directly at variance with the promise in <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.7">2Sa 9:7</reference>, “I will restore thee all the land of Saul thy father,” and the statement in <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.9">2Sa 9:9</reference>, “I have given unto thy master’s son all that pertained to Saul, and to all his house.” By the words, <hi type="italic">“I have said, thou and Ziba divide the land,”</hi> David retracted the hasty decree in <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.4">2Sa 16:4</reference>, so as to modify to some extent the wrong that he had done to Mephibosheth, but he had not courage enough to retract it altogether. He did not venture to dispute the fact that Mephibosheth had really been calumniated by Ziba, which was placed beyond all doubt by his mourning during the whole period of David’s flight, as described in 2Sa 19:24. There is no ground for Winer’s statement, therefore, that “it is impossible now to determine whether Mephibosheth was really innocent or not.”
entries.5d388eea604f7a249b72f065c72f4470506e417a: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.31">2Sa 19:31</reference> <hi type="italic">Barzillai comes to greet David.</hi> - 2Sa 19:31. Barzillai the octogenarian “had also come down from Roglim and gone across the Jordan with the king, to escort him over the river.” את־בּירדּן is the portion in, or over, the Jordan. את is the sign of the accusative, “the piece in the Jordan,” and no further. This is the correct explanation as given by Böttcher, after <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> and Maurer; and the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> היּרדּן is a bad emendation.
entries.1e8d7473e56a982c004019c6b0bd3d91cce7f9e8: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.32-2Sam.19.37">2Sa 19:32-37</reference> <div eID="gen4526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4527" type="x-p"/> As Barzillai had supplied the king with provisions during his stay in Mahanaim (שׁיבה for ישׁיבה, like צואה for יצואה, and other words of the same kind), because he was very wealthy (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. great), David would gladly have taken him with him to Jerusalem, to repay him there for his kindness; but Barzillai replied (2Sa 19:34.), “How many days are there of the years of my life (i.e., how long shall I have yet to live), that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem? I am now eighty years old; can I (still) distinguish good and evil, or will thy servant taste what I eat and drink, or listen again to the voice of the singing men and singing women? and why should thy servant be yet a burden unto my lord the king? Thy servant would go over the Jordan with the king for a short time (i.e., could not remain long with him), and why does the king wish to repay me this favour?” ישׁב־נא: “Let thy servant return, that I may die in my city (my home), at the grave of my parents; and behold thy servant Chimham (i.e., according to the explanation given by Josephus, Barzillai’s son, who had come down with his father, as we may infer from 1Ki 2:7) may go over with my lord the king; and do to him what seemeth good to thee,” i.e., show him favours at thy pleasure.
entries.8efd2c37f6158a8e516172acf8a025dbf3d7e8e7: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.38">2Sa 19:38</reference> <div eID="gen4527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4528" type="x-p"/> David consented to this, and said, “All that thou desirest of me I will do to him.” בּחר with על is a pregnant construction, signifying to choose and impose, <hi type="italic">“choose upon me,”</hi> i.e., the thing for me to grant thee.
entries.2b479768ad82c22f2d473d2eb244adc34742a576: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.39">2Sa 19:39</reference> <div eID="gen4528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4529" type="x-p"/> Thus all the people went over the Jordan; and when the king had crossed over, he kissed Barzillai (to take leave of him: vid., Rth 1:9); and he (Barzillai) blessed him, and turned to his place (returned home). Barzillai only escorted the king over the Jordan, and the conversation (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.31-2Sam.19.38">2Sa 19:31-38</reference>) probably took place as they were crossing.
entries.395235cf4a1fbbc6b80bd7ded27438fb7df94ee8: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.40">2Sa 19:40</reference> <hi type="italic">Quarrel between Israel and Judah about the restoration of the king.</hi> - 2Sa 19:40. David went across to Gilgal (in the plain of the Jordan: <reference osisRef="Josh.4.19">Jos 4:19</reference>), and <hi type="italic">Chimham</hi> (<hi type="italic">Chimhan</hi> is a modified form for <hi type="italic">Chimham</hi>: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.37">2Sa 19:37</reference>) had gone over with him, and all the people of Judah had brought the king over (the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> העבירוּ is an easier reading than the <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> ויּעבירוּ, “and as for the people, they had,” etc.), and also “half the people of Israel,” namely, beside the thousand Benjaminites who came with Shimei (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.17">2Sa 19:17</reference>), other Israelites who dwelt in the neighbourhood.
entries.9c23684a7a6fb8a93b383dc503675db5de20290c: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.41">2Sa 19:41</reference> <hi type="italic">All the men of Israel</hi>, i.e., the representatives of the other tribes of Israel, came to meet the king in Gilgal; and being annoyed at the fact that the men of Judah had anticipated them, they exclaimed, “Why have our brethren the men of Judah stolen thee away?” i.e., fetched thee thus secretly without saying a word to us. <hi type="italic">“All David’s men”</hi> were all his faithful adherents who had fled with him from Jerusalem (2Sa 15:17.).
entries.8a6f5db99e0c22e218d98ead5f2d28cc923718d5: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.42">2Sa 19:42</reference> <div eID="gen4529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4530" type="x-p"/> The men of Judah replied against (על) the men of Israel: “The king stands near to us” (inasmuch as he belonged to their tribe), “and wherefore then art thou angry at this matter? Have we eaten from the king (i.e., derived any advantage from our tribe-relationship to him, as the Benjaminites did from Saul, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.7">1Sa 22:7</reference>), or received anything for ourselves therefrom?” נשּׂאת is an infinitive <hi type="italic">abs. Niph.</hi> with a feminine termination, borrowed from ה;ל literally, <hi type="italic">“or has taking been taken for us.”</hi>
entries.2d7eaae55c2412fc939b89a16b106a00aa91a8b9: <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.43">2Sa 19:43</reference> <div eID="gen4530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4531" type="x-p"/> The Israelites were annoyed at this answer, and retorted, “I (Israel) have ten portions in the king, and also more than thou in David; and wherefore hast thou despised me?” They considered that they had ten shares in the king, because they formed ten tribes, in opposition to the one tribe of Judah, as the Levites did not come into consideration in the matter. Although David was of the tribe of Judah, he was nevertheless king of the whole nation, so that the ten tribes had a larger share than one tribe. הקלּתני refers to the fact, that Judah took no notice at all of the tribes of Israel when fetching back the king. וגו ולא־היה, <hi type="italic">“and was not my speech the first to fetch back my king?”</hi> (On the fact itself, see <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.10">2Sa 19:10</reference>-11.) לי is an emphatic dat. commodi, and is to be taken in connection with להשׁיב, notwithstanding the accents. “And the speech of the men of Judah became fiercer (more violent) than the speech of the men of Israel.” With these words the historian sums up briefly the further progress of the dispute, for the purpose of appending the account of Sheba’s rebellion, to which it gave rise.  <chapter eID="2Sam.19"/> <div eID="gen4531" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p>AND it was told Joab <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">By his Messengers, upon their return.</ns0:note>, Behold, the king weep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth and mourneth for Absalom.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And the <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">

                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And the people gat them by stealth that day into the city <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Not openly, and orderly, and triumphantly, as Conquer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ors use to do; but secretly, and disorderly, and asunder, as if they were afraid and ashamed, lest <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> should see them, and look upon them with an evil eye, as those that had an hand in the killing of his dearly beloved Son.</ns0:note>, as people being ashamed steal a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />way when they flee in battel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 But the king covered his face <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">As a deep mourner, as one that desired neither to see, nor to be seen by any others.</ns0:note>, and the king cried with a loud voice, O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And Joab came into the house <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Either the Gate-house: or, his now dwelling<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />house in the City: to which he was retired, that he might more freely ind<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                        </ns0:gap>lge himself in the expressions of his grief.</ns0:note> to the king, and said, Thou hast shamed this day the faces of all thy servants <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">By disappointing their just hopes of praises and rewards, and by requi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ing them with contempt and tacit rebukes.</ns0:note>, which this day have saved thy life, and the lives of thy sons, and of thy daughters, and the lives of thy w<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ves, and the lives of thy con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cubines <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">All which <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> struck at, and had sooner or later actu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ally taken away, if he had not been cut off in such a man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner without expecting thy knowledge or consent: and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore thy carriage towards them that have saved the lives of thee and thine, with the utmost hazard of their own, is high<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly unjust and ungrateful.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> by loving, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> In that thou lovest thine enemies, and ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />test thy friends; for thou hast declared this day, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> that princes, <ns0:hi>or</ns0:hi> servants, <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> not to thee.</ns0:note> that thou regardest neither princes, nor servants: for this day I perceive, that if Absalom had lived, and all we had died this day, then it had pleased thee well <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This is not to be understood as exactly true in the rigour of it; but onely comparatively and Hyper<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>olically spoken. For <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> desired their preservation and <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s too: but it must be considered, that <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> was now in an high transport of passion, which might easily hurry him into indecent ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressions; and that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s carriage gave too much colour to such a suggestion; and that such sharpness of speech was in a manner necessary to awaken the<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> King out of his Le<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thargy, and to preserve him from the impendent mischiefs.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Now therefore arise, go forth, and speak <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to the heart of thy servants.</ns0:note> comfortably unto thy servants: for I swear by the LORD <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This Oath was either assertory of what he believed might in reason be expected, as likely in great measure to come to pass; or else promissory; or rather, minatory of what he by his influence could and would effect; and if so, it was much more than became him to say to his Sovereign; and could onely be excused by the circumstances which at this time might make it seem necessary: For <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deed to blame in taking no more notice of their good service (however <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> might be faulty also in disobeying the Kings express command as to <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s person); and great reason there was that <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> did now advise, should shew himself less displeased to the people, who had exposed their lives to preserve him and his.</ns0:note>, if thou go not forth <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To the Gate, to shew thy self to thy people, and kindly and thankfully to acknowledge the good service that they have now done thee.</ns0:note>, there will not tarry one with thee this night <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The hearts of all thy people will forth with be irrecoverably alie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nated from thee, and they will look out for some other person on whom they may set the Crown.</ns0:note>, and that will be worse unto thee than all the evil that be<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>el thee from thy youth until now.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:264" />8 Then the king rose, and sate in the gate <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">He was come forth out of his retirement, and appeared in publick, on the Seat of Judgment, at the Gate of the City, to receive the Addresses of his people, and mind the Affairs of the Kingdom.</ns0:note>: and they told unto all the people, saying, Behold, the king doth sit in the gate: and all the people came before the king <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">To congratulate him for the Victory, and to prosess their subjection to him. So <ns0:hi>Ioab's</ns0:hi> Speech, though very severe and presumptuous, was, it seems, a word in sea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son, and had that good effect which he designed.</ns0:note>: for Israel had fled every man to his tent.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 ¶ And all the people were at strife <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Quarrelling one with another as the Authors or Abet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tors of this shameful and cursed Rebellion.</ns0:note> through<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out all the tribes of Israel, saying <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Discoursing privately and publickly of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s high merits, which God, being now reconciled to <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> brings afresh to their me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mories, and reneweth the sense of their obligations to their King, which they had lately shaken off. Thus the Crowns of Kings sit faster or looser upon their heads, as God is pleased to dispose of the thoughts and hearts of their peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, which he can turn in an instant which way he will.</ns0:note>, The king saved us out of the hand of our enemies, and he deliver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed us out of the hand of the Philistines, and now he is fled out of the land for Absalom <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Now we come to reflect upon our own actions, we are sensible of our folly and unworthiness in adhering to <ns0:hi>Absa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lom,</ns0:hi> and thereby forcing <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> to fly out of the Land of <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> to the parts beyond <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> for his security.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And Absalom whom we anointed <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Caused to be Anointed by <ns0:hi>Zadok,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Abiathar,</ns0:hi> or some other of the Priests, whom they persuaded or con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />strained to do this office: for this being a Sacred Ceremony, of great reputation, and a likely means to gain the more au<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thority and veneration from the people to <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> as one whom God by his Vicegerent had constituted and set up; and this rite being usual upon all translations of the Govern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment from one person to another in an extraordinary way, as this confessedly was, it is not likely that they would now omit it: though otherwise <ns0:hi>Anointing</ns0:hi> is frequently put for designing or constituting.</ns0:note> over us, is dead in battel <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">And therefore we have no obli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gation to him, and no hope of any thing from him.</ns0:note>: now therefore why <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb. are</ns0:hi> ye silent.</ns0:note> speak ye not a word <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The People of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> speak thus to the Elders of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> as ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pears by comparing this Verse with the next. Seeing their designs for <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> disappointed, they now repented of that undertaking, and were willing to testify so much by their forwardness to bring back <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> and re-establish him.</ns0:note> of bringing the king back?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 ¶ And king David sent to Zadok, and to A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />biathar the priests, saying, Speak unto the elders of Judah <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Who being the first and chief Abettors of <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s Rebellion, despaired of ever obtaining the Kings grace and pardon, and therefore were backward to promote the Kings Restauration.</ns0:note>, saying, Why are ye the last to bring the king back to his house <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">To his Royal Palace at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>? (<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>eeing the speech of all Israel is come to the king, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> to his house <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Even to <ns0:hi>Mahanaim,</ns0:hi> where now the Kings House and Fami<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly is. Thus sometimes one word is taken in divers senses in the same Verse, as <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 8. 22. Or rather thus: about bringing the King back <ns0:hi>to his house:</ns0:hi> For, First, Those words are very fitly and easily understood here, out of the fore<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />going member of the Verse; such defects being usual in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew,</ns0:hi> which is a very concise or short Language. So it is <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 22. 15. and <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 1. 4, &c. Secondly, It seems most reasonable to understand the same Phrase, <ns0:hi>to his house,</ns0:hi> being twice here used in the same sense in both places, to wit, of his House in <ns0:hi>Ierusalem:</ns0:hi> and this is most agreeable to rule, and to Scripture-usage. Thirdly, Thus the words have more Emphasis than the other way: for if the Speech came to the King at <ns0:hi>Mahanaim,</ns0:hi> it matters not whether it found him in his House there, or in the Gate-house, or in the field. Fourthly, <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had no House in <ns0:hi>Mahanaim,</ns0:hi> which could properly be called <ns0:hi>his house;</ns0:hi> as he had in <ns0:hi>Ieru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />salem.</ns0:hi> And then the Parenthesis should close before those last words, <ns0:hi>even to his house,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>even to his own house,</ns0:hi> to wit, that at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>).</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 Ye <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> my brethren, ye <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> my bones and my flesh <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Of the same Tribe, and some of you of the same Fami<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly with my self; and therefore if I should revenge my self of you, which perhaps you may fear I will do when I have fully regained my power, I should but tear my own Flesh in pieces, and hate my own Body, which Nature and Interest obligeth every man to preserve.</ns0:note>: wherefore then are ye the last to bring back the king <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">This delay doth not suit with the relation you have, and the affection you owe to me.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And say ye to Amasa <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s late General; who judging his case, above all others, desperate, might be ready to use all his Interest with that Tribe, to delay or hinder the Kings return.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>Art</ns0:hi> thou not <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> of my bone, and of my flesh <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> My near Kinsman, my Nephew. See 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 2. 16, 17.</ns0:note>? God do so to me, and more also, if thou be not captain of the host before me <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In my presence; or, now whilst I live; lest he should think he promised him onely the reversion of it.</ns0:note> continually, in the room of Joab <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Who, besides his other Crimes had lately exasperated the King by his wilful Murther of <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> contrary to <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s express command; and by his insolent carriage towards him. And therefore the King having now the opportunity of another person who had a greater interest both in <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> than <ns0:hi>Ioab,</ns0:hi> he gladly complies with it, that so he might both chaftise <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> for his faults, and rescue himself from the Bondagein which <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> had hitherto held him. Yet is it not necessary, from those words <ns0:hi>in the room of Ioab,</ns0:hi> to conclude that <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> was to be displaced to make room for <ns0:hi>Amasa;</ns0:hi> but that he might be in like condition with <ns0:hi>Ioab:</ns0:hi> But, what follows in the next Chapter, makes very probable that he was indeed displaced, and <ns0:hi>Amasa</ns0:hi> put in his place.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And he <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either, First, <ns0:hi>Amasa</ns0:hi> by his great influence upon them. Or, rather, Secondly, <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> by this prudent and kind mes<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sage, and his free offer of pardon and favour to them, as if they had never offended.</ns0:note> bowed the heart of all the men of Judah, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Judg. 20. 1.</ns0:note> even as <ns0:hi>the heart</ns0:hi> of one man, so that they sent <ns0:hi>this word</ns0:hi> unto the king, Return thou and all thy servants.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 So the king returned, and came to Jordan: and Judah came to Gilgal, to go to meet the king, to conduct the king over Jordan <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">To attend upon the King in his passage over <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> and to furnish him with conveniences for his passage and journey. See below, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 41, 42.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 ¶ And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 16. 5. 1 King. 2. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> Shimei, the son of Gera, a Benja<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mite, which <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> of Bahurim, hasted and came down with the men of Judah, to meet king Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And <ns0:hi>there were</ns0:hi> a thousand men of Benjamin with him <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Whom he brought, partly to shew his power and inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est in the people, whereby he was able to do <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> either great service, or great disservice: and partly, as intercessors on his behalf, and as witnesses of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s clemency or seve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity, that in him they might see what the rest of them might expect.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 16. 1.</ns0:note> Ziba the servant of the house of Saul <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Who, being conscious of his former a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />buse of <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> and of his Master <ns0:hi>Mephibosheth,</ns0:hi> which he knew the King would understand, designed to sweeten <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid</ns0:hi>'s Spirit towards him, by his great officiousness and for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wardness in meeting him, and congratulating his return.</ns0:note>, and his fifteen sons, and his twenty ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants with him, and they went over Jordan before the king <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">They did not tarry on this side <ns0:hi>Iordan</ns0:hi> waiting till the King came over, as the most of the men of <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> did; but went over <ns0:hi>Iordan</ns0:hi> to pay their respects and duty to the King there, to express their eager and impatient desire to see the King.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And there went over a ferry<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> boat <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Made by the men of <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> for the Kings proper use; besides which there were doubtless many Boats ready for the use of others.</ns0:note> to carry the kings houshold, and to do <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the good in his eyes.</ns0:note> what he thought good: and Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king as he was come over Jordan <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Or rather, <ns0:hi>as he was passing,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>about to pass over Iordan;</ns0:hi> but this was beyond <ns0:hi>Iordan:</ns0:hi> for as he went over <ns0:hi>Iordan</ns0:hi> to the King, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 17. so doubtless he fell down before him at his first coming into his presence the<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e.</ns0:note>;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:264" />19 And said unto the king, Let not my lord impute iniquity unto me, neither do thou remem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 16. 5.</ns0:note> that which thy servant did perversly the day that my lord the king went out of jerusalem, that the king should take it to his heart <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Be affected with it, or excited to Revenge it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 For thy servant doth know that I have sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">I do not excuse my Sin, but with grief and shame Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fess it; in which case the Lord thy God is ready to Pardon Offenders, and so I trust wilt'st thou be.</ns0:note>: therefore behold, I am come the first <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The sense of my former Sin now hath, and whilest I live will make me the first and most forward in all Acts of Duty and Service to thy Majesty.</ns0:note>, this day of all the house of Joseph <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Object.</ns0:hi> He was a <ns0:hi>Benjamite, Chap.</ns0:hi> 16. 5. How then doth he make himself one of <ns0:hi>the house of Ioseph?</ns0:hi> Answ. <ns0:hi>The house of Ioseph</ns0:hi> is here put, either, 1. For the Ten Tribes, which are oft distinguished from <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> and then they are called <ns0:hi>the house of Ioseph;</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 10. 6. But this distinction was not made before the division of the Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple into two Kingdoms: and even after that Division, <ns0:hi>Benja<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />min</ns0:hi> was constantly reckoned with <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> and not with <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />seph,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Ephraim.</ns0:hi> Or, 2. For all the Tribes of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> who are all called <ns0:hi>the children of Ioseph, Psal.</ns0:hi> 77. 15. Comp. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 80. 1. and 81. 5. as well they might, not onely because of <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi>'s Eminency, (the most Eminent Persons and Things being oft put for the rest of the kind) and because the rights of Primogeniture were in a great part devolved up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on him, 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 5. 1. but also because <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> had been as a Father to them, and had nourished them all like Children; as is expressed in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Text, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 47. 12. But in this sence this was not true, for the House of <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> came be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore him, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 15. Or rather, 3. For all the Tribes, ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cept <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> which are conveniently called <ns0:hi>the house of Io<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />seph,</ns0:hi> for the reasons now mentioned, and are fitly distin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guished from <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> because the Rights of the First-born were divided between <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ioseph,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 5. 2. And though <ns0:hi>Benjamin</ns0:hi> after the Division of the Kingdoms was fitly joyned with <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> because then they adhered to that Tribe; yet before that time it was more conveniently joyn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed with <ns0:hi>Ioseph,</ns0:hi> because they Marched under the Standard of the House of <ns0:hi>Ioseph,</ns0:hi> or of <ns0:hi>Ephraim, Numb.</ns0:hi> 10. 22, 23, 24. Whence it is, that <ns0:hi>Ephraim, Benjamin,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Manasseh,</ns0:hi> are put together, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 80. 2.</ns0:note>, to go down to meet my lord the king.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 But Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered and said, Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD's anointed <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The King. By this Expression he minds <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> of his former Zeal against those who offered any injury to <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> because he was the Lord's Anointed, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 24. 6. and 26. 9. and therefore demands the same Justice against <ns0:hi>Shimei</ns0:hi> for his Cursing of the King, which was so expresly forbidden <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 22. 28. and by the Analogy of that Law, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 21. 17. might seem punishable with Death.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And David said, What have I to do with you <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">I do not ask, neither will I take your Advice in this Matter.</ns0:note>, ye sons of Zeruiah <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Implying, that <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi>'s hand was in this Contrivance, or that he suspected it.</ns0:note>, that ye should this day be adversaries unto me <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> That you put me upon things unfit for me to do, and contrary to my present In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terest; for it was <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Interest at this time to Appease the People, and reconcile them to him, and not now to give them any new distast by acts of Severity: for this would make others jealous, that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> will not forgive them neither, but would watch an opportunity to be Revenged on them. You pretend Friendship herein, and would have me take it for an effect of your Zeal for my Service; but in truth you give me such counsel as my Enemies would wish me to follow, that thereby I might awaken the fears and jealousies of my People which are now asleep, and cast them into a second Rebellion: which either <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Abishai</ns0:hi> really de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />signed by this Advice, that so <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> might recover his Place again, and be made necessary for the King's Service; or <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid</ns0:hi> suspected that they did so.</ns0:note>? <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Sam. 11. 13.</ns0:note> Shall there any man be put to death this day in Israel? for do not! know, that <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> this day king over Israel <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Is not my Kingdom, which for my Sins was in a manner wholly lost, just now restored and assured to me? And when God hath been so Merciful to me in forgiving my Sin, shall I now shew my self Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vengeful to <ns0:hi>Shimei?</ns0:hi> Shall I fully the Publick Joy and Glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry of this Day, with an act of such severity? Or, shall I alienate the Hearts of my People from me, now when they are returning to me?</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 Therefore <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 King. 2. 37, 36.</ns0:note> the King said unto Shimei Thou shalt not die <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">To wit, this day, as <ns0:hi>Abishai</ns0:hi> desireth; nor whilest I live, nor by my Hands, as it is repeated and explained, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 2. 8. nor for this Cause alone. For though <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> gave or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der to <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> for his Punishment after his Death; nor was it fit for the Publick Good that such a Horrid Crime should go Unpunished; yet he would not have him Punished for this Fault alone, but for some other Capital Crime, which <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> presumed <ns0:hi>Shimei</ns0:hi>'s Temper would easily betray him to; and <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>'s deep Wisdom would easily find out, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 2. 9.</ns0:note>: and the king sware unto him <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">That he would <ns0:hi>not put him to death with the Sword,</ns0:hi> as it is expressed 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 2. 8.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 ¶ And Mephibosheth the son <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Grandson, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 6. 3, 6.</ns0:note> of Saul came down to meet the king, and had neither dressed his feet <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">By cutting his Nails, and by washing his Feet, which was usual in hot Climates, and very refreshing; and therefore now neglected, as becoming a Mourner.</ns0:note>, nor trimmed his beard <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">But suffered it to grow ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry long, and disorderly, as was usual with many persons in a forlorn, or mournful State.</ns0:note>, nor washed his cloathes <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">His Linnen Clothes. This and the former were signs, that he was a true and obstinate Mourner, that lay'd aside his usual Refreshments: and they are here mentioned as Evidences of the Falshood of <ns0:hi>Ziba</ns0:hi>'s former Relation concerning him, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 16. 3.</ns0:note>, from the day the king departed, until the day he came <ns0:hi>again</ns0:hi> in peace.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 And it came to pass when he was come to Jerusalem <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">So it is supposed, That <ns0:hi>Mephibosheth,</ns0:hi> though he went to meet the King, wanted either Courage, or fit Opportuni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty to speak to the King till he came to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> because of the great Multitudes that Addressed themselves to the King by the way. Though it might more reasonably be thought, that he could not go from <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> to meet the King, as others did, because he wanted conveniencies for his Journey: for <ns0:hi>Ziba</ns0:hi> had gotten all his Lands and Goods, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 16. 4. and it is not likely that he, who would not pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vide him an Ass to Ride on, or to accompany the King at his departure, would now be hasty to furnish him with one to meet the King, to whom he knew he would complain of him. But the Words may seem to be better rendred thus, <ns0:hi>when he went</ns0:hi> (for so the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Verb signifies, <ns0:hi>Ruth</ns0:hi> 3. 7. <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> 1. 3.) from (which <ns0:hi>Praeposition</ns0:hi> is oft understood) <ns0:hi>Ierusalem.</ns0:hi> For there he was, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 16. 3. and having con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinued there, as probably he did, (because he wanted an Ass to convey him elsewhere, and knew not where to be with more safety) he could not properly nor truly be said to have come thither to meet the King.</ns0:note> to meet the king, that the king said unto him, Wherefore wentest not thou with me <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">As Justice and Gratitude obliged thee to do.</ns0:note>, Mephibosheth?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And he answered, My lord, O king, my servant deceived me <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">By carrying away the Ass which I bid him Saddle for me.</ns0:note>; for thy servant said, I will saddle me an ass, that I may ride thereon, and go to the king, because thy servant is lame:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 16. 3.</ns0:note> he hath slandered thy servant unto my lord the king; but my lord the king <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> as an angel of God <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">To distinguish between true Reports and Calumnies; See on <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 14. 20.</ns0:note>: do therefore <ns0:hi>what is</ns0:hi> good in thine eyes.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 For all <ns0:hi>of</ns0:hi> my fathers house, were but <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> men of death.</ns0:note> dead men before my lord the king <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Before thy Tribunal: we were all at thy Mercy: not my Estate onely (which thou hast now granted to <ns0:hi>Ziba</ns0:hi>) but my Life also was in thy Power, if thou hadst dealt with Rigor, and as Earthly Kings use to do with their Predecessors and Enemies Children. For otherwise by the Law of God <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> himself had not deserved to die by <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s hands, as <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> himself confessed: much less his Children, who were not to dye for their Fathers Sins, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 24. 16. But <ns0:hi>Me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phibosheth</ns0:hi> speaks like a Courtier, and like an Orator, aggra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vating Matters against himself, that he might seem to justifie the King's Sentence, and to submit to it; and so insinuate himself into the Kings favour.</ns0:note>: yet <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 9. 7.</ns0:note> didst thou set thy servant among them that did eat at thine own table: what right therefore have I yet to cry any more unto the king <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To wit; for the Vindica<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of mine Honour, and the Restitution of my Estate.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:265" />29 And the k<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ng said unto him, Why speak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est thou any more of thy matters <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">For as <ns0:hi>Ziba</ns0:hi> was present, so doubtless he was not silent, but said and did what he could to make good his former Charge; which must needs occasion many Words before the King. And the King was not now at leisure for long De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bates, and therefore makes an end of the Matter.</ns0:note>? I have said <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">To wit, within my self; I have considered the Matter as far as now I can, and upon the whole am come to this Resolution, wherein I expect that thou and he do both acquiesce. Or, <ns0:hi>I do now say,</ns0:hi> I pronounce this Sentence in the Cause.</ns0:note>, Thou and Ziba divide the Land <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">The meaning is either, 1. The Land shall be divided between thee and him, as it was by my first Order, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 9. 10. He and his Sons managing it, and supporting themselves out of it, as they d<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>d before, and giving the rest of the profits thereof to thee. And to this the following words may well enough be accommodated; <ns0:hi>Yea, let him take all;</ns0:hi> to wit, to his own sole use. Or, 2. The right and profits of the Land shall be equally divided between you. It seems a very rash and harsh Sentence, and very unbecoming <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Wisdom, and Justice, and Gratitude to <ns0:hi>Ionathan;</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ziba</ns0:hi> seems to have deserved Death for falsly Accusing his Master of Trea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son, rather than a Recompence. But the whole Trans<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />action of the Matter is not here set down. Possibly <ns0:hi>Ziba</ns0:hi> might bring plausible Pretences to justifie his Accusation; and it might be pretended, That <ns0:hi>Mephibosheth</ns0:hi> neglected the trimming and dressing himself onely in Policy, and that for a season, till <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and his Family had Destroyed one another by their C<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>vil Wars, and giving him a fit op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />portunity to take the Crown. So that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> might really be at a loss what to determine. And <ns0:hi>Ziba</ns0:hi> had given proof of his Affections to <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> by an Act of kindness which could not be without hazard to himself, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 16. 1, 2. which <ns0:hi>Mephibosheth</ns0:hi> had not done. And possibly, th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>s was onely a present Sentence, and <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> resolved to Examme things more throughly when he had more leisure, and then to make a more full and final Determination of the Business; which also he might do, though it be not here Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />corded. For we must not think, that nothing was done and said about such things but what is mentioned in Scri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pture. Besides, <ns0:hi>Ziba</ns0:hi> being a powerful man, and the Crown not yet firmly fixed upon the King's Head, <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> might think fit to suspend his Final Sentence till a more conveni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ent season, and not now to provoke him too much by ta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />king away all his Estate from him at once, but to proceed against him by degrees. Howsoever, this is certain, we can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not pass a right Judgment upon this Action of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s, un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />less we understood all the Circumstances of it, which we cannot pretend to do.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 And Mephibosheth said unto the king, Yea, let him take all, forasmuch as my lord the king is come again in peace unto his own house <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">I am contented to lose all, being fully satisfied with the happiness of seeing my dear and dread Soveraign restored to his <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> own, and Truth and Peace returned to his King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 ¶ And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 King. 2. 7.</ns0:note> Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim, and went over Jordan with the king, to conduct him over Jordan <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">And then to cross <ns0:hi>Iordan</ns0:hi> again, and so return to his Native Land.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 Now Barzillai was a very aged man, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> fourscore years old, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 17. 27.</ns0:note> he had provided the king of sustenance while he lay at Mahanaim: for he <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> a very great man.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 And the king said unto Barzillai, Come thou over with me, and I will feed thee with me in Jerusalem.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="34">34 And Barzillai said unto the king, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> how many days <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>he years of my life?</ns0:note> How long have I to live, that I should go up with the king unto Jerusalem <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Seeing my time of continuance in this World is but short, it is not advisable to change my Habitation, or to give thee or my self any further trouble.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="35">35 I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> this day fourscore years old: <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> can I discern between good and evil? can thy servant tast what I eat or what I drink? can I hear any more the voice of singing-men, and singing wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />men <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">My Sences are grown dull, and uncapable of relishing the Delights of the Court. I am past taking Pleasure in delicious Tasts, or sweet Musick, and other such Delights of the Court.</ns0:note>? wherefore then should thy servant be yet a burden unto my lord the king <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">I am through Age both <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />densome to others, and therefore most improper <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> Court<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />life.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="36">36 Thy servant will go a little way over Jor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dan <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">A little onward in thy way to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> and then re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />turn.</ns0:note> with the king: and why should the king re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />compense it me <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>recompence me,</ns0:hi> to wit, for my small kindness to thee at <ns0:hi>Mahanaim,</ns0:hi> which was but a part of my duty to thee.</ns0:note> with such a reward?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="37">37 Let thy servant, I pray thee, turn back again, that I may die in mine own city, <ns0:hi>and be buried</ns0:hi> by the grave of my father, and of my mother: but behold thy servant Chimham <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Barzillai</ns0:hi>'s son, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 2. 7.</ns0:note>, let him go over with my lord the king, and do to him what shall seem good unto thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="38">38 And the king answered, Chimham shall go over with me: and I will do to him that which shall seem good unto thee: and whatsoever thou shalt <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> ch<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>se</ns0:note> require of me, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> will I do for thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="39">39 And all the people went over Jordan: and when the king was come over, the king kissed Barzillai, and blessed him, and he returned unto his own place.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="40">40 Then the king went on to Gilgal, and Chim<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ham went on with him, and all the people of Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dah conducted the king <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Attended upon him on his Journey towards <ns0:hi>Ierusalem.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and also half the peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple of Israel <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Whereas the Men of <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> came intirely and unanimously to the king, as is noted here, and above <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 14. the <ns0:hi>Israel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ites</ns0:hi> of the other Tribes came in but slowly, and by halves, as being no less guilty of the Rebellion, than the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Iudah;</ns0:hi> but not encouraged and invited to come in by such a particular and gracious Message as they were. And this is here mentioned as the occasion both of the Contention here following, and of the Sedition, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 20.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="41">41 ¶ And behold, all the men of Israel <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">To wit, such as were present.</ns0:note> came to the king, and said unto the king, Why have our brethren the men of Judah stolen thee away <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Conveyed thee over <ns0:hi>Iordan</ns0:hi> hastily and privily, not expecting nor desiring our Consent and Concurrence in the Business, which we were no less ready to afford than they. It is also a secret Reflecti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on upon the King, for permitting this Precipitation.</ns0:note>, and have brought the king and his houshold, and all Davids men <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> All thy men; such changes of Persons being most frequent in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Language; thine Officers, and Guards, and Soldiers. This is mentioned as an aggravation of their fault, That they did not onely carry the King over <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> but all his Men too, without asking their Advice.</ns0:note> with him over Jordan?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="42">42 And all the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, Because the king <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> near of kin to us <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Of the same Tribe with us, and therefore both oweth the more respect to us, and might expect and challenge more respect from us.</ns0:note>: wherefore then be ye angry for this matter? have we eaten at all of the kings <ns0:hi>cost?</ns0:hi> or hath he given us any gifts <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">We have neither sought nor gain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed any advantage to our selves hereby, but onely discharged our duty to the King, and used all Expedition in bringing him back, which you also should have done, and not have come in by halves, and so coldly as you have done; See <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 40.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="43">43 And the men of Israel answered the men of Judah, and said<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> We have ten parts <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">They say but <ns0:hi>ten,</ns0:hi> though strictly there were Eleven; either, because they accounted <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> (which comprehends both <ns0:hi>Ephraim</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Manasseh</ns0:hi> under it) for one Tribe, as it is sometimes reckon'd; or because <ns0:hi>Simeon,</ns0:hi> whose Lot lay within the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> were joyned with them in this Action.</ns0:note> in the king <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In the Kingdom, and the ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nagement of the Affairs of it; the Word <ns0:hi>King</ns0:hi> being put for <ns0:hi>Kingdom,</ns0:hi> as it is 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 23. 20. and <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 23. 15. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 7. 17. <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 10. 15. Or, in the King's person, and the disposal thereof.</ns0:note>, and we have also more <ns0:hi>right</ns0:hi> in David than ye <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">As in the general we have more right in the King and Kingdom; so particularly, we have more right in <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> than you, because you were the first beginners, and the most zealous promoters of this Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bellion: and as <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> is nearest of kin to you, so he hath been most injured by you; howsoever, as he is King, we justly Claim a greater Interest in him, than you; inasmuch as we are the far greatest part of his Subjects.</ns0:note>: Why then did ye <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> set us a light.</ns0:note> despise us, that our advice should not be first had in bringing back our king <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">That we being the far greater Number, should not have the first and chiefest Vote in this Action. But the Words are by some, and may well be rendred interrogatively, <ns0:hi>And was not my word first about bringing the King back?</ns0:hi> Did not we make the first mention of it, before you could be drawn to it? For so indeed they did, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 11. And therefore the neglect of their Advice herein might seem more inexcusable.</ns0:note>? And the words of the men of Judah were fiercer <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stead of mollifying them with gentle words, they answered them with greater fierceness and insolency; so that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> durst not interpose himself in the matter.</ns0:note> than the words of the men of Israel.</ns0:p>
